PREFACE 
IN presenting this volume of the Epigraphia Zeylanica to the public, the 
Editor has to express his regret at the delay that there has been in its pro-
duction owing to various unavoidable circumstances. 
Foremost among them 
is the difficulty of the task which the Editor had to perform singlehanded in the 
midst of University duties and his anxiety to obtain the best possible results, 
regardless of all personal inconveniences resulting from postponement of publi-
cation. 
The delay would have continued, had it not heen arrested by the 
present Archaeological Commissioner of Ceylon in supplying the Editor with the 
material needed for the last part of the present volume. 
The Editor hopes 
that th~ same spirit of co-operation in research work will be continued in the 
future to enable him to produce the Epig-raphia Zqlanica regularly in a style 
commensurate 
with the expenditure 
that is being incurred 
thereon 
by the 
Government of Ceylon. 
The Editor wishes to avail himself of this opportunity 
to express his 
profound indebtedness to Professor A. B. Keith for the final revision of his work. 
The Ceylon Government is indeed fortunate in receiving the free assistance of an 
eminent scholar of Professor Keith's world-wide reputation. 
The Editor has, moreover, taken the liberty to dedicate this volume to his 
erstwhile chief, l\Ir. H. C. P. Bell, as a small token of gratitude for his services 
in the cause of Ceylon epigraphy by having initiated the publication of the 
Epi'g·raphia Zeylanica some thirty years ago, as stated in the preface to the first 
volume. 
Finally the Editor's thanks are also due to the Oxford University Press for 
bestowing their usual care in the production of this volume. 
His indebtedness 
to various scholars who have generously given him the benefit of their knowledge 
will be found duly acknowledged in the body of the work. 
The Index being a continuation 
of that appended to Vol. I includes all 
the words and proper names in the two volumes. 
DON 
MARTINO 
DE ZILVA WICKREMASINGHE. 
LO?mON ScHOOL OF ORIENTAL 
STunrns, 
June, 1928.

No. 1. KIRICALLAVA 
PILLAR-INSCRIPTION 
K
IRIGALLAVA 
is a hamlet in Kat;iawat Korale, about twenty miles north-
north-east of Anuradhapura. 
The inscribed pillar was discovered 1 by Mr. H. C. P. Bell in 1892. It is 
about 5 ft. high a:1d 9½ in. square. 
Each of the first three sides contains fifteen 
lines of writing within ruled spaces, the fourth has twelve lines ending with the 
figures of a crow and a dog 2• 
The letters, one to two inches in size, are very well preserved. 
They 
represent the alphabet of the tenth century, but their type is a mixture of that 
of Kiribat-vehera 
and of Morago<;la pillars 3• 
As in th1; former and in the 
records of Kassapa V, Dappula V, and some of Mahinda IV, the two vertical 
s~rokes of the letters a, r, and the medial vowel u are written separately so that 
their lower ends do not meet. 
This is a later type 4, while the ak~aras ka, ma, ya, and la have the older 
forms occurring in the Morago<;la, lripinniyava, and Rambava pillars 5• 
Judging 
from the form of script taken as a whole, the date of our record must be earlier 
than the Kiribat-vehera, but later than that of iripinniyava, and this would fall 
within the period covering the reigns of U daya I and Kassapa IV (circa 952-
980 A.D.). 
As regards orthography, attention may be drawn to the forms mekapparii 
for mey-kappar 8 and melas'in for me/a/sin, melak~zn, melatszn and melattz in other 
lithic records 7• 
Periiliikkan and dunuma(tcjlan are fresh additions to the list of 
obscure technical terms such as perenaf/iyam, melafszn, etc., occurring in Ceylon 
inscriptions. 
The expression abhi,~eka dz (side D, line 2), which obviously

secration, such as anointing (abhifeka) 2• 
The· subject-matter 
is the granting of the usual immunities to a village 
called Itnaru-gama 
in Amgam-kuliya 
by decree of His Majesty Abha 
Salamevan 
in Council in the second year of his reign. 
The State Officials 
who carried out the order were (a) MaI,1itila Kiliyem and (b) Ga:nguJhusu 
Ag-boyim of the family of Mekappar-Vadarum 
3 Vadura 4, and (c) Kavasila:ng 
Gavayim 
of the family of the Chief Secretary Araksama 
Kasba. 
Nothing 
is known about these three officers except that, as the first two were descendants 
of Mekappar-Vadarum Vadura, they must have been related to Ataragalu Kotta 
and Mulava<;la Sakara who set up the atta,,:vi pillar at Morago<;la in the sixteenth 
year of Kassapa IV (963-980 A. o.). The Chief Secretary Araksama Kasba 
may perhaps be identified with the minister Daru Kassapa, a contemporary 
of Vajira (Sinh. Vadura) 5, also a minister of Sena I. 
As to the names of places in the record, we see from the Vevalkatiya slab 6 
that Amgam-kuHya was a district in the Northern Quarter; 
but the village 
I tnaru-gama in it is not mentioned as the property of a temple or other public 
institution as is usually the case. 
This is interesting, for it raises the question 
whether immunities such as those stated in the present inscription used to be 
granted to private lands also or not. 
For two other similar grants, see the 
Noccipotana and the Nagama pillars dealt with below (Nos. 2 and 4). 
We have stated that palaeographically the date of our inscription must 
be fixed in the reign of U daya I or of his successor Kassapa IV, but in 
view of the important information contained in the Timbirivava pillar 7 a~ to the 
biruda title of U daya I being Abha Salamevan 8, while that of his brother and 
successor, Kassa pa IV, was Siri Sang-bo, we are inclined to attribute 
the 
authorship of the present record to Udaya I (952-963 
A. o.). 
And as the 
inscription is dated on the tenth day of the first fortnight of A'sefa (June-July) 
in the second regnal year, it must have been set up some twenty-five years 
before the Morago<;la pillar, ten years before the Timbirivava one, or about 
eight months after the Rambava and Iripinniyava pillars.

No. 3. TIMBIRIVAVA 
PILLAR-INSCRIPTION 
T
IMBIRIVAVA 
is a small village in the Pahala Kalagam Tulana of 
Vilacciya Korale, about twenty-three miles to the west-south-west of 
Anuradhapura. 
The inscribed pillar here is one of those examined by the Archaeological 
Commissioner (Mr. H. C. P. Bell) between 1898 and 1900 1• 
It measures about 
s½ ft. x 10 in. x 9 in., and the writing which covers the first three sides and half of 
the fourt~ is in some parts very much worn, as may be seen from the accompanying 
facsimile (Plate 3). Side A contains twenty-five lines; B,probably twenty-eight, of 
which the last four lines and portions of lines 9, 10, I 5, and 24 are illegible; C, about 
twenty-five lines, of which the first three and the last five are wholly illegible ; 
while D seems to have only eight lines, the last two of these being illegible, and 
the first and sixth partially so. 
The ak!jlaras, one to three inches in size, belong to the alphabet of the tenth 
century A. n., and closely resemble the type of the letters in the Moragoc;la pillar 2 
of the sixteenth year of Kassapa IV (963-980 A. n.). 
The style of the language, too, is in agreement with this record, the first 
twelve lines in both being almost the same word for word. 
There is, therefore, 
no doubt that Kasub Siri Sang-bo,described in both as the brother of Uda Abhii, 
the conqueror of Ruhul}.a and Mala-~a:r)4ulu, is one and the same person, 
namely, Kassapa IV, as stated above on p. 201 of Vol. I. 
The present record gives the biruda title of Uda (Udaya I) as Abhii 
Salamevan. 
This information is important, as it, added to what we already 
know from other sources, enables us to make the inference that the kings· of 
this period followed a certain method in the use of the bz"rudas Sa!amevan and 
Siri Sang-bo. 
No one king seems to have used both the titles ; and if one was 
known as Salamevan, his successor was called Sz"ri Sang-bo, and vice versa. 
To 
take the kings of the tenth century in order, Sena I (circa 897-917 A. n.) had 
the bz"ruda name Salamevan

NAGAMA 
PILLAR-INSCRIPTION 
N 
AGAMA is at present a 'Moor' 
village in Nagampaha Korale, about 
twenty-five miles south of Anuradhapura. The inscribed pillar, measuring 
about 4½ ft. by 8} in. square, stands now in the premises of the Mosque. 
Its top 
is broken off. Mr. H. C. P. Bell, the Archaeological Commissioner, examined it 
in 1895 4• The writing covers all its four sides, twenty-one lines on each, including 
the two top lines that are missing. 
The ak~aras, one to two inches in size, are well incised within horizontally-
ruled spaces .. These represent the alphabet of the tenth century A. D. 
The 
letters a, k, r, and the medial vowel u, have open lower ends. These, as well as 
m, y, l, etc., closely'"l"esemble the type of the characters in the Kirigallava, 
the Noccipotana, and the Morago<;la pillars of Udaya I (952-963 A. D.) and 
Kassapa IV (963-980 A. D.). · On palaeographic grounds we have no hesitation 
in ascribing this grant to Kassapa IV, especially as all the records we know 
of his successor Kassapa V show a distinctly later form of script. 
A com-
parison of the letter k alone in the inscriptions of the two kings affords 
sufficient proof: The only other king to whom this record may palaeographically 
be assigned is U da ya I ; but its contents are against such a supposition. 
Uda Mahapal}.anvahanse mentioned therein was most probably the brother
11 
and sub-king of Sena II, who succeeded him as Udaya I. 
And it is highly 
improbable that he would speak of himself merely as M ahapii without any

Besides, the chronicles of this period make no reference

If the above identification of the king with Kassapa IV (963-980 A. D.) be 
correct, the date of the record being the seventh year of his reign, it is six 
years later than the Timbirivava pillar, and nine years earlier than the 
Moragoc:la one. 
The language 
is, as is usual, similar in style to other tenth-century pillar 
edicts. Vle may, however, draw attention to the honorific term vahanse occurring 
in A, line 8. 
This is the earliest instance of its use in inscriptions so far as we 
know at present 1• The expression hasin pamalJU ko/ shows that in the tenth 
century, A. D. seals were affixed to documents conveying lands 2• 
As to orthography, 
note the forms maha-pa and mahaya, Ag-boy-arak~a-
ma1J,an for Ag-boy-arak-sama~zan, probably through the engraver's ignorance of its 
correct etymology 3, rat-kol for rad-kol, and melatti for the more common mela/st. 
The contents of the record deal with the grant of the usual immunities 
to KoJayunugama, a village which had been given by Uda Maha.pa to one 
(KiJtambava. Mahaya 4 as pama1J,U or 'descendible' property.:. As. a rule, atta1J,i 
pillars of this kind were set up in lands beloi:iging to temples or other public 
institutions. 
But in the present instance, as well as in the two cases at 
Kirigallava 
and Noccipotana, the immunities were granted apparently 
to 
private lands, unless, of course, these were so well known as temple lands, 
that special reference to this fact in the inscriptions was considered unnecessary. 
As to Uda Maha.pa, we have already identified him with king Udaya I. He must 
have been mahapa 4 of Sena II when he made the grant of land to Kitambava., 
who was afterwards, that is at the date of the inscription, a mahaya under 
Kassapa IV. 
Nothing, however, of this minister or of those State Officials who 
set up the pillar can be gleaned from the chronicles, although some of their 
titles and names, such as Mekappar-Vadarum, 
Mugayin 
(P. Moggallana), 
Kiling, Maha!e, Kufu/asala, etc., are familiar enough to us from other inscriptions.

See remarks

As regards the ak~ara ya, we see that from 
the very earliest times two types were in use in the Brahmi alphabet. 
One 
was evidently formed by commencing with the left or right limb (most probably 
the former) ::ind drawing the style or pen up the central vertical line. 
Then 
after thickening its top a little the pen is brought down to make the other 
side limb as in w. In the other type the vertical line was written first and 
the bottom curve afterwards 3 as in ..L. That these ·two ways of forming ya 
prevailed in Ceylon in'"the tenth century A. D. may be inferred from the two types 
of this character occurring in the lithic records. 
The form cu in the Kirigallava 
pillar 4 and in the slab of Kassa pa V 5 near the ' stone canopy' in Anuradhapura, 
as well as the modern co is the development of the first method, whilst the 
type et, in the Iripinniyava 6 pillar and in the present one is that of the second.

The subject of the inscription is a gr~nt of certain immunities by king 
Siri Sa:iig-bo and his Council in respect of Kerela,-gama, a village belonging 
to the hospital built by the Commander-in-Chiet Bena opposite the nunnery 
called Mahindarama on the High Street of the Inner City [of Anuradhapura]. 
The five State Officials who set up the altii1Ji pillar proclaiming the 
mandate of His Majesty in Council are not known to us from other sources; 
but the Commander-in-Chief Sena is clearly no other than llanga Sena, the 
sena-pati of the army of Kassapa IV. 
The pillar-inscription at Ayitigevava 1 
places this identification beyond doubt, for there we read that the nunnery· 
Tissarama, the building of which is ascribed in the 11-fahiivanzsa (eh. Iii. 24) 
to Ilang~ Sena, was erected by the Commander-in-Chief Sena. 
The chronicle 
speaks of him as a prince of the royal family, and gives a detailed account 
of his charitable acts. 
Besides the Tissarama nunnery which he built for the 
sisters (bhikkunis) whom he appointed to have the care of the Maricavatti 
Thupa and the Great Bodhi-tree, he erected several religious edifices such 
as the Dhammarama, Kassapa Sena, Hadayunha, and Samuddagiri. 
He also 
established hospitals (vejja-salii) at Anuradhapura 
and Po}onnaruva for the 
prevention of pestilential diseases, as well as dispensaries .(bhesajja-geha) in 
divers places in the capital. 
To these institutions he granted fruitful lands 
and gardens with keepers. 
The present inscr:ption records the building of 
another hospital which is not mentioned in the Mahavamsa account. 
The 
location of this hospital in close proximity to the 11-ft'hind-aram (P. Maht'n-
diiriima) nunnery suggests that it was either meant for the exclusive use of the 
nuns or that these devotees, like the nursing sisters of the present day, attended 
on the patients, succouring the sick being a veyyavaccam (Sinh. vatavat), one of 
the ten meritorious acts which Buddhism imposes upon its votaries 2• 
The High Street Mangul-maha-veya of the Inner City is also referred 
to in the slab-inscription of Kassapa V 3,near the 'stone canopy' at Anuradhapura, 
as the locality where this king established royal hospitals (raj-ved-hal) and thus 
allayed the fear of diseases.

Since then another inscription on a slab, measuring 5 ft. 3 in. by 3 ft. 3 in.,

It is engraved in 44 lines 
of writing in small Sinhalese script of the eleventh century A. D., but the letters 
are so worn that the two ink-estampages before me do not admit of a reading 
good en.:mgh for publication. 
So much of the text af has been made out shows 
that it is a samvata-paha~ta 'edictal stone' containing rules for the management 
of the hospital 1 attached to the monastery. 
Here and there we read interesting 
terms, such as ved-hal-kami'yan, 'employees of the hospital,' ved-hal-dasun, 'serfs 
of the hospital,' ved-sam-daruvan, 'State physicians,' ved-hal-bad-gam-bim, 'villages 
and lands attached to the hospital,' ved-hal-bad-kut/in, ' tenants attached to the 
hospital.' 
Had this record been legible, it would have doubtless given much 
valuable information concerning public hospitals to which the Ceylon chronicles 
make frequent but scanty references. 
The inscription on the pillar (6 ft. by 12½ 
in. square) is, on the other hand, 
in fairly good preservation. 
It covers all the four sides, A, B, and C having 
26 lines of writing, and D I 7 lines with the figures of a crow and a dog 
below two others of which one looks like that of a va/ajata, 
' Buddhist 
monk's fan,' while ·the other, according to Mr. Bell, represents a sickle. 
The akitiaras belong to the alphabet of the tenth and early eleventh 
centuries A. D. 
Their size varies from one to one and a half inches each, and 
their type is practically the same as that of the slab records of Kassapa V 
and Dappula V with the exception of ma, which retains here, as it does even 
in some later records, the 'archaistic' form.

MAPIRIGIRIYA 
PILLAR-INSCRIPTION 
The language is the same in style as that of Kiribat-vehera, iripinniyiiva, 
and other tenth-century inscriptions of the kind. 
The contents 
tell us that king ·Abba Salamevan 
was a son of Mayuri-
dunu Siri Sang-boy by the twice-anointed queen, and that, under a decree 
of his Supreme Council, in the third year of his sovereignty, three Officers 
of State, namely, (a) Mekappar Asaholu Mihindu, of the family of Pal).~i-rad 
Dapu.lu, (b) Sumeragamu 
Sata, probably of the same family, and (c) KutuJ.asali 
Kit, of the family of the Chief Secretary Kasha Araksamai;ia, came and granted 
certain immunities in respect of the land within the four boundaries 
of 
Ma4iligiri-Atveher
1-Piyan-gala in Rantisa in the district of Bidervatu-kuliya. 
The nature of the privileges agrees in the main with other similar records of . 
the period. 
There occur, however, some new words and expressions in addition 
to those already familiar to us, of which the full signification is not very clear. 
They are d•11#-maefula, probably 'those belonging to the archery department,' 
du11uva-balat 
2, 'captains of the bowmen,' vela-yut-pas-dena, ' the five engaged 
in the supervision of fields' (?), and siindive de-utu-kiri. 
The order that 'dead goats and fowls' should be given to the hospital 
attached to the Vihara shows that animal food was allowed in these Buddhist 
institutions under certain restrictions. 
Obviously the regulation rexers to 
animals killed by accidents. 
The present record undoubtedly belongs to Kassapa V (980-990 
A. o.), 
and is only three years earlier than this king's inscription near the 'stone 
canopy' in Anuradhapura 
3• 
Both the documents agree not only in the type 
of the script but also in the historical facts that he bore the biruda title AbhA. 
Salamevan 4, that he was the son of Siri Sang-boy (Sena II) by a twice-anointed 
queen 5, and that he took an interest in the establishment of hospitals. 
The 
title Mayura-dunu applied to his father has not been found elsewhere. 
It may 
either be the birth-place of Siri Sang.boy 
(Sena II) or may have reference 
to a traditional ancestry. 
Of the places mentioned in our inscription, Rantisa may be identified with

J-\.

The 
pillar was examine..~, 
1. by the Archaeological Commissioner (Mr. H. C. P. Bell) 1 
and myself in 1892. 
All its four sides are inscribed on, 
Side A contains 
eighteen lines of writing, with the figure of a va/iijata carved in relief below; 
B, twenty lines, followed by the 6gure of a dog ; C, seventeen lines, with a symbol 
which,· according to Mr. Bell, represents a sickle; and D, ten lines, with the 
emblems of sun, moon, and a crow. 
The letters are well engraved, and are about one to two inches in size. 
They represent the alphabet of the latter half of the tenth century A. D. and in 
type resemble mostly those in the Mac;Iirigiriya pillar 2 of Kassapa V. 
In both 
these records the letter m retains its 'archaistic' form, while in regard to a, r, 
and the medial vowel u, the present pillar differs from the other in the use of 
the older type with closed lower ends. 
The language is the same in style as that of other atlatp: pillars of the 
period; but t~ere q,ccur in this inscription several hitherto unknown technical 
expressions of which the real meaning is at present obscure. 
These are (saba)rd 
kabali, suambura (paddala) kabalz', se?J,a, tol-(or kol-)pap£n, val-(or pal-)gattan 
3• 
The subject-matter 
is a grant of the usual immunities to a certain plot 
of ground, five payalas in extent, belonging to Tisaram (P. T-issarama) nunnery 
built on the 'Auspicious High Street' (Maftgttl Maha-veya) by the Commander-
in-Chief Sena. 
1 His report runs:-' 
Ayitigevewa.-A 
well-preserved pillar, still standing, with an inscription 
of sixty-five lines: figures of dog and crow and symbols cut in relief below. The letters are mostly 
well incised. The record belongs to the fifth year of "Abha Salamewan." 
'Near are remains of the brickwork and some pillars of the ancient vihare, in front of which has 
been erected a small modern temple (Kandyan type) on stumps of broken columns of the old shrine. 
Lying prone at the site of the ancient vihare was found the trunk, armless and footless, of a standing 
Buddha; and close by, the head in excellent preservation. 
The joggle-holes in the neck, hands, and 
ankles of the trunk and in the head proved that the feet and other members had (as usual with these 
standing images) been separately carved and attached. 
The circular pedestal with the feet block was 
unearthed amid the brick debris in its original position. With. infinite labour the statue was set up 
in situ. It stands 9 ft. 6 in. from head to pedestal.'-A. 
S. C. Annual Report for 1892, pp. 6-7.

HILST 
exploring the ancient sites in Vilacciya Korale in 1896, the 
Archaeological Commissioner (Mr. H. C. P. Beli) came upon this pillar 7 
(6 ft. by I ft. square) at Bilibava in lhala Ka.Hi.gam Tulana, about fifteen miles 
to the south-west of Anuradhapura. 
Three of its sides are inscribed on, A con-
taining 27 lines, B 31, and C 22, followed by the figures of a dog and a crow. 
Those of sun, moon, and va/apata (Buddhist monk's fan) mentioned by Mr. Bell 
must be on the fourth side. 
To judge from the two estampages before me, 
the letters do not appear to have been deeply engraved on a properly prepared 
surface. 
The ak~aras, 1 to 1½ 
in. in size, belong to the alphabet of the lafter half 
of the tenth century. 
They resemble most the type of letters in the ·Buddha-

nnehala pillar of the third year of Abha Salamevan 1• 
This king has already 
been identified with Kassapa V (980-990 A. n.). The present record confirms 
the identification both palaeographically and historically. 
As it is dated in the 
seventh year of his reign, it is four years later than the Buddhannehala inscrip-
tion, and one year later than the Anuradhapura 
slab-inscription of Kassapa V 2, 
though some letters, such as a, k, m, and r in the present pillar, are more archaic 
in type than those of the slab. 
The language is the same in style as that of other tenth-century records 
familiar to us, the first nineteen lines of the text agreeing, word for word, with 
lines 1-16 
and 22-24 
of side A of the Ellevava pillar 3 of Dappula V, half-
brother.4 of Kassapa V. 
Attention may, however, be drawn to the technical 
expression ek-tan-samiyen vanda vada/eyin avud (B, lines 11-13) which occurs 
in most of the inscriptions of this period, but with some variation or other, 
e.g. vada/a ek-tau-sam£yen a 6, vadii/eyi"n 8, vadafeyin a 1, vadiif ein avud 8, vada/en 
a;,-ud', vada/q£n sabhayen a 10 , vada/a ek-ti:in-samiyen sabhayen ii 11, vat-him£yan 
tk-tan-samiyen vada/ey£n 12, and vandi:i vadaf ey£n 13, 
In ordinary speech vandi:i (P. vanditva) means 'having worshipped' with 
closed palms placed on the forehead. 
Whether it means thi!' here or not it is 
difficult to say. 
It is, however, interesting to note that this form of showing 
respect is observed even to-day amongst Sinhalese country folk in conversing 
with a superior. 
Possibly members of the King's Council used the sail'~ 
formality in giving their assent to the proposed decrees. 
The expressions 
ve!a-yut pas-deni'i (B, lines 29-30),pereliikkan(C,lines 
1-2), and (sand£ve) de-utu-kiri 
(C, lines 5~6} are still unintelligible.

give us the usual particulars of a grant of immunities to 
llahagipiyova, 
a village in the district of Pirivatu 
in the Southern Quarter,

The king Abha Salamevan, of our record is, as stated above, identical 
with Kassapa V (980-990 A.n.), the inscriptional notices of his parents being 
in agreement with those of the chronicles 1• 
Sak-Senevi 2 was his son, and 
the Kasub-Senevirad-pirivena 
may be the building referred to in the Maha-
varhsa 3 as the ' delightful parive1Ja which he called 1.fter his own name, and 
gave it unto the Theriya [i.e. the Mahavihara] brethren with lands'. 
If this 
be the case, the full name of the son of Kassapa V must have been Kasub 
Sak-Senevi Sa:iigalnavan. 
The five State Officials who took part in the grant are not known to us 
from other sources. 
The name Budim, however, occurs in the Ellevava pillar.

pi'n-para, the village-road of .Ataviragollava, about eleven miles from 
Mqdawacci in Ka<;lawat Korale. 
It is inscribed on all its four sides, but owing 
to the splitting of the stone at the top several lines on sides A and D are 
obliterated. 
Judging from the height of the pillar, side A may have contained 
more than eighteen lines, or else the space above the writing must have borne 
a Buddhist emblem. 
Side B has twenty-eight lines; C, twenty-five, surmounted 
by a figure of the sun; and D, seventeen, with figures of a crow, a dog, 
a Buddhist monk's fan (va/apata), and a so-called sickle. The inscription was 
first read by Dr. Goldschmidt 1• 
Dr. Muller published a rough transcript, with a 
translation of the first side only, in 1883 2• 
The Archaeological Commissioner 
(Mr. H. C. P. Bell) re-examined it in 1890 8• 
The characters, half to one and a half inches in size, belong to the alphabet 
of the last quarter of the tenth century A. D. 
In type they resemble, more or 
less, the letters in the Puliyanku!am slab of U da Mahaya 4, dated the twelfth year 
of Dappula V (991-1003 A. D.). 
The language is in keeping with the style of other similar records of the 
period. 
The .text 0n side A agrees with that on side A of the Ellevava 6 and of 
the foregoing Bilibava pillars almost word for word. 
Attention may also be 
drawn to the use of van in B, lines 1 3 and 18, and vara in line 2 2 1 instead of the 
fuller and more familiar form vara van. 
Among the various classes of people 
prohibited from entering the protected village are some names of obscure 
meaning, and not of frequent occurrence in inscriptions. 
These are ulavacfu, 
arakkan, peralakkan, dunuva-balatun (captains of bowmen?), da/£-gattan (net-
men ?), (y)amu,zguru-gatuvan 
(mace-men ?), and tuf;t/i'se. 
The contents tell us that king Abha Siri Sa:ng-bo ransacked the Pa.Q<;lya 
country, and obtained a victory in the ninth year. of his reign, that his son was 
Abha Salamevan, and that in the tenth year 6 of this king's sovereignty, the 
immunities mentioned in the record were granted to the village Velangama 
belonging to the Sirisangbo-rad-pirivena, 
and an atta?J,i' pillar was set up to

No. 11. MA YILAGASTOTA 
PILLAR-INSCRIPTION 
T 
Ii IS quadrangular pillar, measuring about 6 ft. x I I in. x 7 in., was discovered 
by Mr. J. H. Dawson, the Irrigation Officer at Mayilagastota, a village 
about eight miles from Tissamaha.ra.ma in the Hambantota district. 
Dr. P. 
Goldschmidt examined it and published a short account of it with a portion of 
the text in 1876 •. The pillar was subsequently brought to the Colombo 
Museum where it now lies. 
The inscription covers three sides of it, but that on the third side is not 
legible. 
The first two sides contain thirty-five lines each. 
• 
The letters belong to the alphabet of the tenth or early eleventh century A. D. 
Their size varies from ¼ to 1¼ 
in. each, and their type 4 is that of the Vessagiri 
slab of Mahinda IV 5• 
The language too agrees with the style adopted in the shorter inscriptions 
of this king, and its phraseology is nearly the same as that of his pillar-inscription 
at Attanaya.la-viha.ra 6 in the same Hambantota district.

As mentioned before, the inscription was first read by Dr. Goldschmidt, and 
then by Dr. Muller who published a transcript and_ a translation of it with a short 
preliminary note in his Ancient Inscriptions in Ceylon (No. 120). 
The subjoined 
edition_ of the text has been carefully prepared with the aid of ink-impressions 
supplied by the Archaeological Commissioner (Mr. H. C. P. Bell). That it 
differs considerably from the former will be apparent on a comparison of the 
two versions and their English translations. 
Both Goldschmidt and Muller found this .record most useful in identifying 
Mahinda 
IV of the Mahavamsa with Siri Sa:iig-boy Abahay 
of the Mihintale 
tablets. 
Though this identification has now been found to be correct. yet the 
facts which they were able to adduce at the time were not sufficient to prove the 
identity of Mahinda IV, still less that of his parents 1• 
The present reading of 
the inscription, however, gives the link which these scholars desired so much. 
I have elsewhere 2 stated reasons for supposing that Mahinda's father, the great 
king Abha or Abahay Salamevan or Siri Sang-bo Abha (or Aba), may have been 
either Dappula V or Kassapa V. 
This can now be settled definitely, for on 
side A, lines 12 to 16 of the record, there appear distinctly the names of king 
Abha Salamevan 
and queen Sang 3 Gon-biso 
as those of the parents of 
Mahinda. 
The former is identical with Kassapa V4, who bore this biruda, and the 
latter with his queen Sangha, the beautiful daughter of the sub-king (Mahinda) 5• 
A confirmation of this relationship may be inferred from the. statement in the 
Mahavamsa (liii. 51 and liv. 48) that Mahinda IV's matula, i. e. his mother's 
(namely Sangha's) brother (probably half-brother), was king Udaya III who died 
whilst engaged in re-building the palace called Ma9i, that the army of the Co!a 
king had destroyed with fire. 
Touching the children of the sub-king Mahinda 
(brother of king Sena II) the Mahavanisa (Ii. 15-18) says that by his p~incipal

wife Tissa he had a daughter named Sangha who became queen of Kassapa V, 
and by his other wife Kitti: he had one daughter and four sons of whom 
Kittaggabodhi 
was the governor who raised a rebellion in RohaQ.a (!. c. 94). 
About the other three sons the chronicle is silent, but from the Puliyarr-kulam 
slab-inscription 1 it appears certain that king U daya I I was one of them. 
The 
Pujavaliya says that king Sena III was a brother of Udaya II. 
So he must be 
identical with the third son, and the fourth was obviously king U daya I II 
referred to as the matula (maternal uncle) of Mahinda IV. 
The accompanying genealogical table, which I have prepared from data 
derived from inscriptional and other sources, will enable the reader to form an 
idea as. to how the Ceylon kings of the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth centuries A.D. 
were related to one another. 
The contents 
of the present record deal with the dedication of certain 
lands to Uc,.&-Tisa-pirivena situated near Mahagama 
on the left bank of 
Kirind-ho and with an enumeration of the immunities which usu~lly form an 
important feature of such grants. 
No date is given, but it is dear from the use of the title apa that the grant 
was made when king Mahinda IV was a mere governor, b~fore be was raised 
even to the rank of mapa (mahaya), or yuva-raja; by Sena IV (circa 1023-
ro26 
A.D.). 
This would, therefore, be during the early part of Mahinda's 
career, probably when he was ruling RohaQ.a, of which Mahagama mentioned 
in the record was the capital, and the U <;la-Tisa-pirivena in question was 
close by. 
The village which still bears the name Magama or Mahagama lies on the left 
bank of the Magama or Kirinde river (Kirifzdu-hoya or-oya ), not far from the ruins of 
Tissamaharama, north-east of Hambantota. 
Moreover, in his interesting report on 
Tissamaharama 
2, Mr. H. Parker says that U c;la Tihawa (i. e. U c;la-Tisa-vava) is 
well known at Tissamaharama as the name of the upper part of Tissa tank and 
that it once formed a separate tank, the bund of which is now to be seen inside the 
present Tissa tank. The pirivena, he adds, may have stood between the adjacent 
river and the tank, as attested by the remains of some building which are reported 
to exist in the jungle to the west of the upper part of the Tissa tank. 
As to 
Dr. Muller's suggested identification 3 of U <;la.-Tisa-pirivena with U ddhakandaraka-
vihara built by Mahanaga 4 (ci'rca 200 
B.c.), 
definite proof is still wanting.

RAMBAVA 
SLAB-INSCRIPTION 
R
AMBA. VA is a V!,ell-known village in Kanda-korale at the junction of the 
two main roads from Anuradhapura and from Mihintale, about nine miles 
to the north-east of the former town. 
It should not be confounded with the 
village bearing the same name in Kuficunu Korale, some twenty-five miles further, 
where lies the fine pillar-inscription of king Abhaya Salamevan (Udaya I) dealt 
with in Vol. I, article No. 13. 
The present slab was discovered by the Archaeological 
Commissioner 
(Mr. H. C. P. Bell)1 in r892, while on tour during the second quarter of the 
year. 
It has since been brought into Anuradhapura. 
The inscription covers a ruled surface of 4 ft. 7 in. by. 2 ft. 6 in., and contains 
thirty-nine lines of writing more or less worn by the action of the weather. 
The letters are on the average 
half to one inch in size, and closely 
resemble the type of the alphabet of the Veva.lkatiya slab 2 of Mahinda IV 
(drca 1026-1042 
A.D.). 
The long e in the word vahanse (line 27) of the present 
record, and the long o inyona in the Vevalkatiya pillar clearly show that already 
in Mahin~a's ti,tr1e the vertical virama sign was in use to indicate a long vowel~. 
The language 
follows the style usually adopted in l\1ahinda's slab-
inscnpt10ns. 
The first six lines, moreover, and also several phrases in the body 
of the text, agree word for word with those in the two records• of this king at the 
so-called J etavanarama 
5 in Anuradhapura. 
The date is the tenth day of the bright half of the lunar month Vap 
(Sept.-Oct.) in the first regnal year of king Siri Sang-bo Abha (Mahinda IV, 
drca 1026-1042 
A.D. or W. 975-991 A.D.). 
In the foregoing article on the Mayilagastota pillar I put together all the 
historical facts I could find bearing on the parentage of this king, with the result 
that it became almost evident that he must have been a son of king Kassapa V, 
1 His reference to it is as follows :-

the " Cooly Shelter" at Rambewa, and copied as much of the writing as is legible. The record almost 
certainly belongs to Mahinda IV (975-991 A.n.), though the name of the king has worn off the stone.' 
(A.S.C. Annual Report, 1892, 
p. 6.)

RAMBA VA SLAB-INSCRIPTION 
who died according to the Mahavamsa thirty-five years and seven months before 
Mahinda IV's accession to the throne. There arises now the question whether or not 
he is to be identified with Mahinda, the son of Kassapa, who successfully quelled 
a rebellion raised by Kittaggabodhi in Rohaq.a, and became the governor of that 
province, which he ruled during the reigns of U daya I and Kassapa IV 1• 
The 
inscriptional references 2 to Mahinda IV as conqueror of Rohaq.a and restorer of 
religious monuments there, agreeing as· they do with the Mahavamsa account 
both of this king and of prince Me.hinda, the son of Kassapa, go a great way to 
support the theory that they were one and the same person. 
As against this, 
must be taken into consideration the fact that Mahinda, the son of Kassapa, 
was old enough already in the reign of Uda:,a I 3 to lead a punitive expedition to 
Rohal)a, and that according to the lvfahavainsa reckoning Mahinda IV's accession 
to the sovereignty took place some sixty-three years later~ So, if the two princes 
are identical, Mahinda IV must have been at least eighty years old when he became 
king, and ninety-six when he died. 
This is very improbable, and in view of the 
strong support from inscriptions in favour of the identity, I am inclined to fall 
back upon the theory that either the text of this portion of the Mahavamsa as we 
have it at present is faulty, or its author got confused regarding the traditional 
dates of this period, and miscalculated the length of the reigns ;f some of the 
kings that preceded Mahinda IV, as I suggested on p. 157 of Vol. 1 4 when 
discussing the Buddhist era in Ceylon. 
The contents 
of the record deal with the grant of certain lands, with the 
immunities usually attached to such grants, to one Kiliiigu-rad 
Pirivat Ha:m-
buvan, to be held by him and his descendants for the purpose of supplying oil 
to illuminate the stone image of the Buddha at the Sacred Bodhi-tree. 
The 
statue is probably the one mentioned in the Jetavanarama slab, No. 1, line 26 5• 
Of the four ministers of Mahinda IV's Council who proclaimed this grant, 
Xu<;].asala Vatkami-detim 
figures also in the Vessagiri grant of this king. 
The others are not known to us from other sources.

3, and the latter that of

Both these names were in common use in the twelfth cen-

The language is Sanskritic Sinhalese with the exception of that of the 
last three lines, which contain a Sanskrit stanza in the beautiful Sragdlzara 
metre. 
In phraseology and general style ~t approaches very much the modern 
literary form, and agrees so much with the other known inscriptions of Kirti-
Nissanka-Malla, that I am inclined to attribute the authorship of all of them 
to one person. 
Sinhalese inscriptions often give the names of the officials or 
members of the Curia regis who were sent out ·with full powers to proclaim the 
mandate of the King in Council. 
In Indian records such an officer is technically 
called dutaka 5, while the composer and the writer or engraver are respectively 
termed kartr 6 and lekhaka 6._ Ceylon inscriptions make no mention of the last 
two classes of officials, and yet they must necessarily have been in existence.

In line 27 there is a curious allusion to a class of fowlers called Kambodi. 
King Nissailka-Malla presented them with gold and cloth and whatever other 
kind of wealth they wished, and ordered them not to catch birds. 
Neither 
Rhys Davids nor Muller give any explanation whatsoever regarding them in their 
articles 2 on this inscription, while Mr. H. C. P. Bell identifies them with the 
Kambojian mercenaries who, he thinks, were employed by the Sinhalese kings 
at this period 3• 
This identification is based, I believe, on the similarity of the 
two names, but it must be remembered that the Kambojians of PoJonnaruva, 
whether they were monks, ambassadors, architects, or even mercenaries (as he 
surmises), must have been devout Buddhists. 
The inter-communication that 
existed between Cambodia and Ceylon during the eleventh, 
twelfth and 
thirteenth 
centuries, and that led to one of the gates of PoJonnaruva being 
called Kamboja-vasala was more or less of a religious character ; and I have 
so far not found a single allusion in the literary or inscriptional records 
of the Island pointing to the immigration of non-Buddhistic clans from Cam-
bodia. Mr. Burrows was, therefor.e, quite right in wondering why the Kambodin 
of the present record, if they belonged to those who came over from Cambodia, 
should have been specially addicted to killing birds. 
And he was also on the 
right track in the solution of the problem, when he drew attention to a passage 
in Fergusson's History of lndi"an and Eastern Archi"tecture supporting the local 
tradition that the Kambojians of Cambodia originally came from the north-west of 
India, and suggesting that Ceylon may have formed a half-way house 4• 
In 
the Asoka inscriptions 5 and in some of the other Indian records the Kambojas 
are almost always mentioned together with the Yavanas as if they were t_ribes 
dwelling in close proximity to one another.

while the Yavanas (Ionians), we know, were originally the Asiatic Greeks 1• 
Both these names came in later times to be applied in a loose way to foreigners

For example, we find four references to 
Yavanas in the Mahavamsa. 
The first is in the compound word yonasabhaga-
vatthu (eh. x, v. 90 of Geiger's ed.). 
It is true that this is a doubtful case. 
Nevertheless, if the compiler of this portion of the Mahavainsa, who probably

may have thought of the Yavanas as a ciass of foreigners for whose use king

necessarily Greeks) 
on the north-west frontier of India, as suggested 
by 
Mr. V. A. Smith in speaking of those referred to in the Asoka edicts (A soka,

during his successful campaign in Southern India under

They were u::1doubtedly Mussulman 
settlers who used to trade or were still trading all along the west. coast from 
the Persian Gulf down to Ceylon, and possibly further east. • They are called 
in Tamii f:OJJ,akar (a~11a!T&ir), 
no doubt from Pali or Pkt. yonaka. 
Their repre-
sentatives in Ceylon bear the Sinhalese name yona (pl. yon or yonnu), a deri-
vative of P. yona, or more likely yonaka. 
Like them the Kambojas also may 
have entered India and Ceylon by land and sea, probably in pursuit of their 
trade in horses. 
The reference in the Varhsa Brahmal)a to a certain Kamboja 
Aupamanyava as a pupil of Madragara points, according to Prof. Macdonell and 
Dr. Keith 2, to 'a possible connexion of the Madras 3, or more probably the 
Uttara 11adras, with the Kambojas, who probably had Iranian as well as Indian 
affinities'. 
The Kambohs of the present day in the NW. Provinces of India are 
(Iconographie bouddhz'que, p. 134), while Langdon identifies them with' the well-known Aramaic people 
Gambula, who appear in the annals of Asarhaddon 681-668 
B. c. and are spoken of by the Arabic 
geographers in the Middle Ages. They were an important and powerful people who occupied the 
region east of the·mouth of the Tigris along the Persian Gulf eastward towards Elam'.

supposed to be their descendants. 
Rajendra Lala Mitra 1 calls them ' a turbulent, 
crafty, stiffnecked race, and, as such, more akin to Afghans than to any of the 
meek Hindu races of the plains of India'. 
Like the Ya vanas of yore and the 
Y ol)nu or Ceylon Moors of the present day, the Kambojas also shaved their 
whole head 2, and references to Kamboja horses as late as the twelfth century A. D. 
are not wanting in South Indian literature 3, 
It is, therefore, not impossible that 
just as the Afghans of modern times, the Kambojas also may have come to Ceylon, 
probably as horse-dealers, and a colony of them ma'.y have settled permanently 
in Anuradhapura in company with the Yavanas when that city was in the zenith 
of its glory. 
They were, of course, not Buddhists, and, as such, it was not sur-
prising that in the twelfth century A. D. their descendants, probably by Yavana 
or low-caste Sinhalese wives, having become poor, eked out an existence as 
fowlers, and were regarded as a spetial tribe of bird~catchers. 
I do not think 
they can be connected with those Buddhist monks, ambassadors and others who 
from time to time came over to Ceylon from Cambodia as a result of long friendly 
intercourse between the two Buddhist kingdoms. 
Finally, a word or two about the present text and translation of the 
inscription. 
They have been prepared from the two ink-estampages supplied 
to me by the Archaeological Commissioner, and are quite independent of those 
alreaciy publish~d by Professors Rhys Davids and Muller respectively in].R.A.S., 
vol. vii (1875), and in A.I.C., as No. 145. Previous to these scholars, the 
Interpreter 
Mudaliyar of the Courts at Anuradhapura 
made for the first time 
a translation of the inscription, which he contributed to the Ceylon Observer for 
December 29, 1874. All of them, however, omitted to translate the Sanskrit 
stanza which, as I mentioned before, may possibly help us to settle the question 
of the authorship of all the inscriptions of king Kirti-Nissanka-Malla.

heritage, under one canopy of dominion. 
And [seeing that] many persons,. 
Qppressed by the excessive and illegal punishments inflicted by king Parakrama-
Bahu, the Great 1, in violation of the customs of former sovereigns, and being 
[thereby] impoverished, are eking out an existence by robbery, and [reflecting that]

he ga~e them his patronage. 
Desiring that what he 2 had given should not only 
be maintained but also be increased, he graciously remitted taxes for several

HE so-called Hata-da-ge-1, 'the Shrine of Sixty Relics', is the ruined vihara 
marked No. 4 in the inset (B) of the accompanying 
plan of the 
Polonnaruva ruins, which has been reprod'iiced here from the plans given in the 
Archaeological Commissioner's Annual Reports to enable the reader to form an 
idea as to the situation of the inscriptions dealt with in the following pages and 
the character of the ruins in which they are found. 
In 1885, whilst removing the debris from this shrine, Mr. S. M. Burrows 
discovered three _inscriptions 2, two in the shrine itself and one in the porch. 
The last is the present record. 
It is boldly engraved in twenty-three lines on 
the smoothed and ruled surface formed of two slabs fitted together edgeways, 
one above the other, on the right side of the passage through the portico 3• 
The letters cover a qua?rangular 
area of 5 ft. 3 in. by 3 ft. 8 in. of this 
surface. 
They are on the average one inch to one and a half in size. 
Their 
type is practically the same as that of Nissai1ka-Malla's other inscriptions . 
..

a detailed and lucid description of each separate building, Mr. H. C. P. Bell writes as follows:-
' The cluster of ruins excavated during the season of 1903 is situated directly east of T6pavl:wa tank, 
and north of the Citadel and the isolated Hindu temple hitherto miscalled "Da/ada Maligawa ". 
This i~ the most varied and important group at PoJonnaruva.

So too are the orthographical peculiarities and the general style and phraseology 
of the language 1• 
The inscription begins with a Sanskrit stanza in tri#up salin'i metre and 
ends in a Sinhalese quatrain, rather poor in composition. 
Both of these contain 
Nissanka-Malla's appeal to future kings to protect and preserve the Dharrna. 
The rest of the record mentions (a) king Sri Jaya-Gopa and queen Parvati 
as his parents, Simhapura in the Kaliiiga country as his birth-place, and the 
heir-apparent Vira-Bahu and princess Sarva:nga-Sundari as his children; 
(b) some of his administrative and charitable acts, such as the suppression of 
lawlessness, the remission of taxes for five years, the yearly distribution of gifts 
of value amongst the people, the granting of security of life to animals that live 
in forests and tanks, and his tours of inspection throughout the country; (c) his 
successful expedition to South India and the tribute he received from the Cola 
and the PaQQya kings; and finally (d) the building in stone of the Vata-geya 
'Rotunda', 
the !lisaa>ika-lata-m~4&paya 'Nissaiika flower-trail hall', and the 
lliaaiaka-dalada-geya 
'Nissaiika tooth-relic house', which Messrs. Bur_rows 
and Bell have identified with the ruins 2 marked N os. 12, 9, and 4 of inset (B) in 
the accompanying plan.

No date is given in the inscription. 
We know, however, from other 
sources that Kirti.:Nissanka-Malla 
reigned from about September, 
1187, to 
1196 
A.D. 
His record at the Ruvanvali-dagaba 
(above, p. 73) tells us that he 
visited that shrine in his fourth regnal year (i.e. between September, 1191, and 
August, 1192), 
but in its glowing account of his doings no allusion whatsoever 
is made either to his tours of inspeGtion in Ceylon or to his expedition to 
South India. 
From this we may infer that the present inscription, as well as 
others which expressly mention these two events of his reign, may have been 
set up after the fourth year, namely between I 192 and 1196 
A.D.

HE front wall of the vestibule or pro-naos of the so-called Hata-da-ge 1 
which is probably id~ntical with the Nissanka-da}adage mentioned in 
the foregoing inscription 2 was composed of a series of 'dressed slabs of all 
sizes fitted together dry, but so closely as to defy the inroads of vegetation. 
The plainness of this wall face is relieved most artistically by a double border, 
vertical as well as horizon_tal, of faintly incised carving-a 
band of ha1nsas (swans) 
with another of leafy vignette' 
3• 
The inscription occupied a quadrangular area (about 3 ft. 4 in. by 6 ft.) of the 
outside face of this wall, on the right of the entrance. 
The accompanying facsimile 
(Plate 16) shows a portion of the ornamental border at the base and on the right 
side. 
The ak~aras which vary from one to one and a half inches in size are 
engraved in seventeen horizontal lines along ruled spacing of the smooth surface. 
The form of script and the peculiarities of orthography and style of composition 
of the record are practically the same as those of the foregoing slab. 
The contents, however, give us some additional information regarding 
Kirti-Nissanka-Malla (1187-1196 A._D.). He is here styled Sirilhapuresvara 
Lamkesvara KaliJiga-Cakravarti, of which the first two birudas are not 
included in those mentioned on p. I 24 of Vol. I. We are also told that he 
began his tours of inspection in the second year of his reign, and that he made 
journeys throughout Ceylon, including places difficult of approach, such as 
Samano!&• (Adam's Peak), in the course of which he corrected 
various 
administrative irregularities. 
He, moreover, fixed the distance of a gavu 5, and 
calling it a Nz'ssanka-gavu he set up inscribed- milestones in their proper places. 
His inscription at the Ruvanvali~dagaba 6 which was incised in or after 1191 A. D. 
makes no mention of his tours to distant parts of the Island.

And consequently the palaces and pavilions enumerated in

as the .context seems to indicate. 
Reference is made in line 4 to a ma{i'gava (palace) built by a former king in 
seven years and seven months. This was most likely one of Parakrama-Bahu I's. 
If we may read between the lines, Nissanka-Malla was evidently struck with the 
architectural beauty of the mansion, but was too proud to utilize it. So he built 
another of seven storeys (sat-vana-mal-ma{igava), probably a poor imitation of it, 
in forty-five days. 
I am inclined to identify the former with the famous ruin 
called sat-mahal-prasadaya 1 'seven-storeyed palace'.

TRANSLATION. 
[Lines 1-4.] Hail! 
His Illustrious Majesty Simhapuresvara 
Lailkesvara 
Xaliilga-Cakravarti, from the second year of his accession to the sovereignty, 
toured round Lanka, thoroughly inspecting, like a nelli fruit on the palm [ of his 
hand], villages, market towns, capital towns, and many other localities of note, 
as well as those places difficult of access either on account of water, marshes, 
forests or mountains such as Samanola (Adam's Peak). 
And he freed the 
kingdom from the thorns of lawlessness so thoroughly, that a woman might even 
carry a casket filled with the nine [kinds of] gems and not be asked, 'What is it?' 
Thus did he keep [Lanka] in a peaceful state 1• 
[Lines 4-9.) Thereafter having beheld a palace which had been erected in the 
capital forinerly in seven years and seven months, and thinking 'it befits us to sit 
only in a palace built by a king like ourselves', he erected within forty-five days 
a palace of seven storeys. 
He built also a magnificent ma~ujapa (pavilion) from 
which to watch fights, and he watched the elephant-fights (from it). 
Including 
the strong .... 
hall 2, he erected three thrones and furnished them with gates, 
ramparts, &c. 
He built of stone three ma1J,fapas (pavilions) so that they might 
last a long time, and formed the Kaliilga Park 
like anotJier VeJuvana 3• 
He got him queens from various countries, such as Kaliilga, Ve:ngi, Kari;i.ata, 
Gurjara, &c., and building for them separate palaces of various kinds within 
the premises of the harem gave them much wealth. 
[Lines 9-17.] 
In the three kingdoms he erected palaces and almshouses at 
several places ; to numberless beggars he gave much treasure, such as gold, 
gems, silver vessels 4, &c., and at different places he formed parks and built of 
stone thrones (naming them) Virasimhasana. 
He suppressed various adminis-
trative Injustices. 
In the course of thus inspecting the thre~ kingdoms in 
various ways he fixed [the distance of] a gavu and calling it a Nissailka-gavu, 
he caused inscribed mile-posts to be set up [ each in its place]. 
Thereafter 
His ~lajesty together with Queen Kaliil.ga Subhadra, the sub-queen Kalya:r;ia,

No. 16. 
POI,,ONNARUVA: 
HA TA-DA-GE 
INSIDE 
WALL-INSCRIPTION 
T
HIS inscription was also brought to light in 1885 by Mr. S. M. Burrows, 
who published an incomplete transcript and translation in the C.B.R.A.S. 
'7ournal for 1887. 
Like the foregoing one, it is engraved on a series of slabs 
which were once built into the wall inside the shrine. 
The writing covers 
a quadrangular area, 4 ft. 1 in. by I ft. 6 in. tof the smooth surface and consists of 
eight lines running along ruled spacing. 
The ak~aras which vary from one inch to one and a half in size are 
precisely the sa'.me in type as those of other inscriptions of Nissanka-Malla 
3• 
In respect of orthography 
or the style of composition, there is hardly 
anything that calls for notice. 
The record is a tactfully worded exhortation to 
Buddhist monks to exercise care in the selection of persons for admission 
to the priesthood and to desist from doing things contrary to the teachings of 
the Buddha. 
There is no doubt that the Buddhist monks of the time of 
Nissanka-Malla were not all perfect, and he, like other kings before him, had 
occasion to assert his right as 'Defender 
of the Church' to put down corrupt 
practices.

LOSE to the eastern outer wall of the so-called Hata-da-ge mentioned 
above at page 84, and within a few yards south-west of that remarkable 
edifice known as the Sat-mahal-prasadaya 1, there lies the oblong slab called 
gal-pota 2, 'stone-book', with its ends pointing north and south. 
According to Mr. Bell 3, 'its exact measurements are: length, 26 ft. _IO in. 
down its axis ; 26 ft. 7 in. at both edges ; breadth 4 ft. 7 in., depth varying 
from 2 ft. 2 in. to.I ft. 4 in. 
The upper surface of the slab was first smoothed, 
then framed and divided into three partitions by narrow fillets (1¼ to ! in.) 
horizontal and vertical, in imitation of the bare spaces on the palm leaves of 
ola manuscripts, in which holes are pierced at two convenient points for the 
uniting cord. 
Within these partitions (9 ft., 8 ft. 7 in., 8 ft. 8 in. in width) the 
record was carefully incised in sharply cut letters, in size 1¼ 
in., between ruled 
lines. 
Each partition is read by itself, the text running on from the first line at 
the top left-hand (south-west) corner of the stone slab. 
The inscription of 
seventy-two lines, containing more than 4,300 letters, is by far the longest known 
in Ceylon. 
'Thegaij,ota 
was raised on a brick podium, measuring (average) 31 ft. 3 in. 
by I 3 ft. 6 in., and sheltered by a canopy supported on ten pillars, 5 ft. in height

most p~rfect representations existing of the seven-storeyed temples of Assyria'.

of it, w\th illustrations, see A. S. C. Annual Report, 1903, pp. 14-16.

Note also should be taken of the use of the

locative case for the sake of emphasis as Ramesvarayehi-di (B, l"ine 19). These 
grammatical forms occur rarely, if at all, in earlier inscriptions, though they 
are in common use in modern Sinhalese.

The subject-ilattel 
of the present inscription may be described in the

In my article on this king's Dambulla record 3 I 
touched upon the political factors in force at the time of his accession to the 
throne. 
There were representatives of the Kaliriga-vamsa to which the king 
himself belonged t, of the Sinhalese Govi-kula who were adherents of Parakrama-
Ba.hu I, of the Pa.Q.<;lya 
and probably also of the Cola families, holding influential 
positions at the Sinhalese Court and elsewhere in the island. 
They were all 
perpetually intriguing for political supremacy, and Nissanka-Malla must have 
felt the insecurity of his regal power, and more so of the claims of his dynasty 
to rule after him. 
This is clear from the fact that none of his successors was 
able to hold the sceptre for any length of time. 
They were either assassinated 
or deposed. 
So at the outset of Nissarika-Malla's reign he found it necessary to 
adopt a plan of action by which he hoped to safeguard his interests. 
He had 
one of two courses open to him-either 
a policy of repression or of <;:onciliation-
and he wisely chose the latter which would have met with the success it deserved, 
had it not been for his open antagonism to the aspirations of the nobles of the 
Govi-kula.

Nissari.ka-Malla's · numerous inscriptions tell us how he pursued this policy. 
He took every opportunity to remind the people of the story of the Vijayan 
colonization of Ceylon as given in the Dzpavamsa (eh. ix. 1-31) and in the 
Mahavainsa (eh. vii) and to impress upon them the theory that Vijaya was 
a prince of the Kali:itga-Cakravarti-kula and that, therefore, the throne of 
Ceylon belonged only to this dynasty. 
He asserted, moreover, that the Kalinga 
princes alone were the defenders of the Buddhist Church, that their rufo had 
always been for the benefit of their subjects, and that he himself assumed the 
sovereignty because it was incumbent on him to do so, as he was the rightful 
heir by hernditary succession. 
In this manner he justified his position and 
posed as a sovereign who held his authority entirely for the good of the com-
munity. 
He backed up these assertions by having his various administrative 
and charitable acts recorded in glowing terms not once but many times in 
inscnpt1ons. 
The crowning point, however, of his conciliatory method is in his 
exhortation to ~s subjects in section C, where his theory of kingship is explained 
for their enlightenment. 
And it must indeed be said to his credit, whatever his 
motives might Have been, that, so far as is known, no other king of Ceylon has 
ever attempted :to win the confidence of the public in this manner and play the 
role of a politi9al pbilosopher. 
If we analyse his ideas we see that they are 
H induistic, th,bugh strongly tempered with the cosmopolitan views of the 
Buddhists as; regards the nature of society and the principles underlying 
social relations. 
He agrees with Manu 1 when he says that a king is a god 
in human form 2, but he goes against him in comparing ' an upright king' 
to a Buddha, for Manu believes in the natural inequality of man, while Buddha 
denies it and upholds the doctrine of the equality of man, agreeing in this 
respect with Seneca's theory that 'no one is in truth nobler than anQther,

on the part of the

His contention as to hereditary right, his recognition

in Western Europe in the ninth century, his proposition that in the absence of

landing of Vijaya in Ceylon. 
Accordingly, Nissanka-Malla must have been just 
thirty years old when he ascended the throne in 1187 5 and thirty-nine when 
he died.

in use in

inscription of King Sahasa-Malla

TRANSLATION. 
A. 
[Line 1.] Hail! 
This Dharma, which gives happiness and which alone 
deserves to be honoured by the whole world, should always be preserved. 
Vira-Nissanka-Malla 
makes this appeal over and over again to the rulers of 
the earth in the name of [their} good fame 1• 
[Lines 2-7-] King Vijaya, descended from the family of Kali:nga Cakr&-
vartin who had the power of travelling through the air 2, and who belonged to 
the royal line of the Okkaka dynasty, exalted by [the possession of] an assemblage 
of auspicious and infinitely sublime qualities :-When 
one thousand seven hundred 
years had elapsed since this king, protected by the gods in accordance with the 
behest of the Buddha, arrived in the· Island of Lanka, and destroying the )'akfas 
made it an abode for mankind 3, there was born the great king Siri-Saiigabo 
Kili.nga Parikrama-Bahu 
Viraraja Nissanka-Malla 
Aprati-Malla 
in Simh&-
pura in the country of Kali:nga in noble Dambadiva 4, the birth-place of Buddhas, 
Bodhisattas and Universal monarchs-{he 
was born] of the worn b of the great 
queen Pirvati unto king Sri-Jayacopa 
who was like unto a ·1ilaka 5 ornament 
to this royal line [of the Okkaka dynasty]. 
He grew up in the midst of royal 
splendour, and being invited by the great king of the Island of Lanka, his senior 
kinsman 6, to rule over the Island of Lanka which is his by right of lineal suc-
cession of kings 7, he landed in Lanka in great state. 
Enjoying (thereafter) the 
regal dignities of governor and sub-king 8, and being proficient in the science 
of arms, in religion, and in all arts and sciences, he in due 0rcler of regal 
succession received the sacred unction and wearing the crown assumed supreme 
sovereignty. 
1 See Hata-da-ge Portico slab (lines 1-2), above, p. 89. 
Previous translator!! give ne translation 
of this verse. 
2 See above, p. 89, note 3. 
'This is a reference to the story given in Dv. ix. 1-3 r and in JJfv. vii. 1-45 and alluded te in 
other Ceylon historical works such as the Rajavaliya, the Pujiiv«liya, &c. 
• Skt. Jamburlvipa, India. 
5 See above, p. So, note 8. 
• Kula-je/u = Skt. kula-/yef!ha 'head of the family'.

[Lines 7-12.J His commanding personality is made dazzling to the eyes of 
the world through· the fact that at his coronation festival he by a mere frown 
dispersed the clouds that gathered filling the vault of the firmament. 
His great 
majestic power is such that when hunting in the forest 1 a fierce savage she-bear 
sprang before him with a sharp growl, he laid her and her whelps dead 2 at his 
feet. 
He possesses the powers of a lion-king, which [ can J extract water from any 
spot he likes, for [ on one occasion J when [travelling] in a water-less desert, the 
moment he entertained the thought 'it would be well if there were water', [there 
fell a shower of rain J from an out-of-season cloud [ and] produced an abundant 
stream. 
His power of command is such that it is not transgressible, for instance, 
when [ once J on going to BaJ,1.a 
3 to enjoy sea-sports', 
a huge poloitga 5 
appeared in front of him, he said to it 'thy approach is unwelcome, be off and 
thyself prescribe what [punishment] is meet for thee', 
The serpent then stung 
itself and sacrificed its life. 
He is endowed with a majestic personality, for the 
moment his state elephant saw him, the elephant was so delighted that he roared 
the shout of triumph and offered of his own accord his back [ to ride on]. 
[Lines 12-18.J His Majesty drove away his enemies and gladdened the faces 
of the people just as the sun rising on the Orient Mount dispels darkness and ex-
pands the lotus blooms. Equalling Sakra, the Lord of the gods, in boundless regal 
splendour, the f'¾,11 
moon in gentleness, Mount Meru in firmness, the ocean in 
depth [ of character], and the solid earth in patience, and flourishing like a 'wish-
conferring' tree that has sprung up as a result of the merits of the world, [he thus 
thought to himself]:-'Many 
people in this Island of Lanka, which is the heritage 
of our dynasty, have through the unjust acts of some kings lost their family 
privileges and their wealth.' 
Then, [filled] with great compassion, he restored 
to them their family privileges 6. 
He remitted taxes for five years, and enacted 
a law that in collecting revenue from lands and fields, the excessive taxes

INSCRIPTION 
T
H IS granite seat or asa11a, measuring 3 ft. 7 in. square, with moulded sides::, 
stands 3 ft. above ground in the form of a pedestal a few feet off the south-
east comer of the site (now identified as that of a Pz"(ima-ge 4, 'image-house') 
in 
the group of ruins on the Topa-vava quadrangle. 
The inscription runs round all the four edges of the smoothed upper surface 
of the stone in four lines, the letters, 
I to 2 in. in size, being incised between 
ruled lines which are 2½ in. apart, thus leaving a blank space of 22 in. square in 
the centre 5, 
The record indicates the asana as that on which king Nissanka-Malla 
used to sit whenever he witnessed the dramatic and musical entertainments 
which were held in the Kali:Iiga-vana after his return from his Ceylon tours and 
his Indian campaign. 
According to the inscription in the Hata-da-ge vestibule 
(above, No. 15), this king began his journeys through the length and breadth of 
Ceylon in the second year of his reign, which was 1189 A. D. 
So the seat must 
have been set up at a later date, namely, between Sept. 1189 and Sept. 1196. 
The question as to whether it stands in its original place in the Kali:Iiga-vana, 
'Kalinga-forest ', and whether this locality is identical with the Kali:Iigodyana,

RANKOT-DAGAEA 
PILLAR-
INSCRIPTION 
T
H IS inscription is repeated on each of the four pillars which once supported 
the roof of an open pavilion on the southern terrace of the Ruvanvali 
or Rankot-dagaba 1• 
In the centre of the enclosed space which, according to 
Professor Rhys Davids, was about eight feet square, there must have been 
an iisana, a sort of dais, from which, as the inscription states, the king used 
to pay his adorations to the relics enshrined in the dagaba. 
The four pillars are now fallen, and two of them are broken. 
They are 
about 6 ft. long, I 2½ in. square at top and bottom, and octagonal in the centre 
where the writing is in consequence narrower, being only about 5 in. wide. 
The letters are engraved between ruled lines which are two inches apart 
and vary in size from I to 2 in. Their type is the same as that of the foregoing 
records of N issanka-Malla 2• 
The contents are, as usual, a repetition of some of this king's acts as 
an introduction to the principal statement indicating the purpose for w_hich the 
pavilion was built. 
The date is not given, but it must be placed some time after the fourth

Mahavamsa (lxxiii. 95-112) as the work of Parakrama-Bahu I (u53-1186 
A. o.) 
though manifestly repaired by some of his successors 1• 
The slab on which the present record in 14 lines is cut, formed one of 
the flagstones of the rectangular bath 2• It is now broken into several fragments, 
one of which was found in the Topavava village: the others are missing. 
Nevertheless, we have been able to restore the text easily, as it is the same 
as that of the foregoing Rankot-dagaba pillar-inscription, with the exception 
of the concluding sentence which states the purpose for which the cistern or 
paliisa was used by Nissarika-Malla. 
The date of the record may be placed between 1191 
and 1196 
A.D., for 
reasons given in connexion with that of the Rankot-dagaba inscription. 
The 
letters vary in size from 1¼ to 2½ in. They are well engraved between ruled 
lines 2½ in. apart, and are of the same type as that of the script of the period.

T
HIS 
inscription in five lines covers the upper smoothed surface of a 
quadrangular slab measuring 5 ft. 2 in. by 2 ft. 9 in., which once formed 
the top flagstone of a raised seat. 
Mr. Bell examined it some twelve years ago, 
between 1901 
and 1905
1• 
The slab was then lying inside the ruined shrine 
referred to by him as Siva-Devalaya 
No. 1, and situated a little to the south 
of the main group of Buddhist ruins on the raised quadrangle near Topavava 
tank 2• 
; 
The letters, from half an inch to one inch in size, are engraved, as in 
other asana slab-inscriptions, between ruled lines, one inch apart, running parallel 
to each side of the rectangular slab and leaving a blank space of 3 ft. 8½ in. 
by 1 ft. 6 in. in the centre 3• 
The type of the script is the same as that of 
the other records of Nissanka-Malla. 
The stone is much worn. 
Consequently a considerable portion of the 
inscription is totally illegible, but what remains readable clearly shows that 
the text agrees almost word for word with that of the foregoing stone-bath 
inscription, •the only exception being the concluding sentence which indicates 
the present pedestal seat or asana as the one which Nissatika-Malla 
used 
to occupy when performing the function of lustral bathing (nanu me•) at the 
ceremony of propitiating the nine planetary gods (nava-graha-santi).

HIS quadrangular slab, measuring 
10 ft. by 5 ft. 3 in., lies on the_ ma{ttva 
or terrace of the so-called ' Kiri-vehera' dagaba in Polonnaruva 3, about 
eight or ten yards to the south-east of its south altar. 
As will be seen from the accompanying facsimile\ the slab has an orna-
mental border carved with swans (hamsas) running in a single file from right to 
left along a fillet of foliaged creeper pattern which encloses a rectangular area of 
9½ ft. by 4½ ft. 
Within this and at equal distance from its sides thereis another

rectangle also marked by a fillet engraved with what looks like a conventional 
crab and fish pattern. 
The smoothed space outside the inner rectangle is ruled 
with lines three inches apart, so as to receive between them three lines of the 
first inscription on each of the four_ sides. 
Similarly, the area within this 
rectangle is ruled so as to receive four lines of the second inscription on each 
side, leaving, thereby, a blank space of 6 ft. by I ft. 3 in. in the centre. 
The letters, 
1 to 2 in. in size, represent the type of the alphabet of the 
period, namely, the latter half of the twelfth century A. D. 
The text of the 
first or outer inscription is the same as that of No. 24 above 1, with the 
exception of the concluding clause which indicates the pavilion (kutfama), as 
the one from which His Majesty Kirti Nissanka-Malla worshipped the (Buddhist) 
relics. · The text of the second or inner inscription, of which a faulty and incom-
plete transcript and translation appear in A. I. C., under No. 152, agrees word 
for word with the inscription at the Nissail.ka-lata-mal}.gapa 2, the only exception 
being the final clause stating that the pavilion was built after His Majesty's 
return from the Indian campaign, and that it was used for worshipping the 
(Buddhist) relics. 
It is obvious from both these records and from the few.stumps of pillars 
still existing round the slab 3 that the kutjama or pavilion in question was a 
structure similar in style to the one at Rankot-dagaba 
4 and that it was built 
about the same period, namely, between 1191 and 1196 
A.D. 
The inscribed 
slab must have been the flagstone of a raised seat within it, from which the 
royalty was wont to worship the relics enshrined in the Kiri-vehera-dagaba

NISSANKA-MALLA 
153 
T
H IS quadrangular slab, measuring 3 ft by 2 ft. 7 in. and lying now at the 
premises of the Archaeological Commissioner at Polonnaruva, was brought 
there from the spot where the present rest-house is. 
Its original site is not 
known. 
The first twenty-three lines of the inscription are engraved on the smoothed 
face of the slab between ruled lines, two inches apart 1• 
The next four lines are 
cut; according to Mr. Bell 2, one on each of the four narrow sides. 
The rest 
of the inscription is wanting. 
It may possibly be found on the reverse side of 
the slab. 
The letters vary in size from ½ to 1 ½ in. Their type is the same as that 
of other records of Nissanka-Malla. 
The subject with which the inscription 
is really concerned is given only at the end of the text, now missing, if we may 
judge from the style of composition of other records of the kind. So the portion 
of the text appearing below is only the usual introduction to this subject, and 
contains nothing new. It agrees almost word for word with the inner inscription 
of the Kiri-vehera slab (above, No. 26) and with lines 10-12 
of the Dambulla 
record (E. Z., Vol. I, No. 9). 
Variations in spelling such as viinse for vahanse, riimesvara for riimesvara 
are not uncommon in other inscriptions of this period, namely, the latter half of 
the twelfth century A. D.

[Lines 21-28] 
Considering that grants in favour of those who rendered 
services in various capacities conformable to his wishes should last as long as 
Sun and Moon endure, he did not [ as heretofore] have them written on tal-pat 
(palm-leaves) which were liable to be destroyed by white ants, rats, and the like, 
but had such grants engraved on copper (plates), and so established the practice 
which had not been in vogue aforetimes in Lanka.

with the virtuous qualities of an extraordinary sympathetic nature, he granted

NO, 28]

No. 28. PO~ONNARUVA: 
SLAB-INSCRIPTION 
AT THE 
NORTH-GATE 
OF THE 
CIT ADEL 
157 
T
HIS quadrangular slab, measuring about 6 ft. by 2 ft. 3 in., was found 
completely buried at the North-gate of the ruined citadel 1, where it was 
subsequently placed in an upright position. The inscription covers both its sides 
and is engraved, as is usual, between ruled lines two inches apart. 
The obverse, 
or side A, contains 3 7 lines and the reverse 36-. The letters 
vary in size from 
~me to two inches each. 
They agree with the form of script of the latter half 
of the twelfth century A.D. 
Another slab having the same shape and about 
the same dimension and containing a copy of the present record, similarly 
engraved, was discovered at the East-gate of the citadel. 
Both these copies 
and Dr. ~ltiller's transcript 1 have been utilized in producing the text printed 
here for easy reference with a facsimile (pl. 2 1) of the former slab and an 
improved translation of the text. 
The Sanskrit verse at the beginning and th-at at the end are· in siird11,la-
vikrztjita metre. 
The rest of the inscription is written in. Sinhalese in the 
usually bombastic style of the composer of Nissarika-Malla's records with 
a repetition of his favourite phrases and expressions. 
The subject-matter consists of a p·anegyrical account of Nissanka-Malla's 
virtuous qualities and of his charitable acts, followed by an exhortation similar 
to that given in the Galpota record above, No. r 7, in which he advises his 
subjects to choose for their sovereign a prince or princess of his own Kaliriga 
dynasty. 
He denounces vehemently the aspiration of the Govi caste and of 
the non-buddhistic princes from Cola or from Kerala to the throne of Ceylon, 
emphasizing these sentiments with the threat that all those who join them would 
be treated as traitors and would accordingly be extirpated together with their 
families and their worldly possessions. 
His policy, however, of consulting his 
subjects through the medium of a representative council 3 shows, as I stated 
at p. IOI above, that he did his best to popularize his rule.

royal succession, wore the crown and assumed supreme sovereignty. 
[His 
Majesty] shining like Sakra in boundless regal splendour, and distinguished 
by the assemblage of virtuous qualities [he is endowed with], such as generosity, 
truthfulness, heroism, and the like, dispersed his enemies, even as the sun rising 
over the Orient Mount dispels darkness, and thus he kept the whole Island of 
Lanka in peace. 
Then flourishing like a 'wish-conferring' 
tree that has sprung 
up by reason of the merits of the world, he promoted the interests of the Church 
and the State; and ruling in accordance with the ten principles of regal duty he 
made his residence in the Kalinga royal city of Pulastipura. 
[Lines 17-25] He quenched the fire of poverty with showers of gifts of 
gold, silver, kahavu~ttt 1 pearls, precious stones, clothes, jewellery, &c. 
And 
being pleased when he beheld the prosperity of the people [so benefited], in 
great compassion and wisdom, he reflected, 'We have rendered help to the 
world, for such is the native disposition of our Kalinga dynasty; how can we 
maintain to the end of the present cycle (ka!pa) the stability of this prosperity 
which we have secured as [it were] in the golden age (krta-yuga)?' 
[Lines 2 5-3 7] Then perceiving that utter destruction forthwith befalls the 
wealth, nay the very tribe, of the wicked ones who work e.;il against kings in 
ignorance of the greatness of their virtues-kings 
who stand as gods in human 
form and as parents to the world, His Majesty determined that such destruction 
should not befall any one. 
So he constantly gave much advice and instruction 
as if bestowing eyes on the world blind through ignorance. 
[Further] declaring 
that treason, like the five unpardonable sins 2, is a thing which should not be 
committed, he was pleased to expound [as follows] the law and policy:-
Those who have committed evil acts such as destruction of life and the 
like and those who have taken poison destroy themselves alone, while on 
the other hand treason destroys those who have committed it, together with 
their families and their associates. 
Side B.

mind. 
Moreover, it is not right to live without a king.

INSCRIPTION 
T
HE construction of the new road from Minneriya to Po!onnaruva in I 900 
brought to light a group ~f 'Hindu ruin!'.' about a mile to the north of 
Topavava proper 1• 
In September of the following year the Archaeological 
Commissioner (Mr. H. C. P. Bell) commenced a careful exploration of the site; 
with the result that among other finds he discovered the present inscription 2 on 
the western slope of the long hummock of granite rock which rises there to a 
height of about 60 ft., its length being 270 ft. or more, and its breadth (greatest 
at the centre) 90 ft. 
Th'e inscription is in forty-five lines, covering a smoothed surface (8 ft. by 
8 ft. 3 in.) of the slope of the rock to the left or north of the flight of steps 
leading up to, the building on the top. 
The ak1;1aras are in size 1½ to 2 in. 
They are well incised between ruled lines 2¼, 
in. apart, and are of the same type 
as those of Nissatika-Malla's records described above. 
With the exception of 
portions of lines I and 2, and a number of letters in other parts, the whole 
inscription is quite legible. 
It begins with a Sanskrit verse ia sra,_rdhara metre 
and proceeds in the usual style of language of the period to give an account of 
Nissatika-Malla's birth and parentage, his administrative and charitable acts, 
the religious edifices and alms-houses he built, his tours in Ceylon, the so-called 
invasion of Southern India, and finally the erection of Priti-danaka-ma~<;l.apa, 
'joy-conferring pavilion', and its consecration as a sanctuary whereby every one 
entering its premises had the right of asylum. 
It was to commemorate this last 
act that the present record was inscribed. 
All these details taken in conjunction with those given in the Galpota 
and other inscriptions of Nissatika-Malla 3 yield the following facts :-He 
was 
born in Simhapura in Kalitiga about the year 1157 A.D. 4 ; he crossed over to 
Ceylon at the invitation of his senior kinsman (probably Vijaya-Bahu II) 5, 
sometime between 1180 and I 186; 
he was sub-king 8 to Vijaya-Bahu II in 
1186-1187 and eventually ascended the throne in September 1187, in the 
thirtieth year of his age. 
The first two years of his rule (1187-1189) were 
marked by charitable acts and certain administrative reforms carried out _most
