The account of the Indian campaign, so persistently mentioned in all 
his inscriptions as one of his great achievements, must not be taken as 
literally true. 
Nissanka-Malla neither reigned long enough nor had the time 
{even if he had the ability and t~e men} to carry out successfully such 
a task and also to build the many edifices attributed 
to him. 
The truth 
may be that the composers of his inscriptions in their eagerness to please 
their vain-glorious monarch have magnified his visits to Ramesvara and pro-
bably to some of the South Indian courts, as if they were military expeditions, 
and credited him with the victories gained by Parakrama-Bahu I, a decade 
or so before. 
That this is true in the case of several buildings is the opinion of 
Mr. Bel~ 1• 
Besides, the historical works are absolutely silent as regards his 
Indian expedition. 
In fact they have dismissed his reign in a short paragraph 
without even telling us whether at the expiration of his nine years' rule 
in September 1196 A. D., he died a natural death in his thirty-ninth year of age 
or fell a victim to a party plot brewing at the time in spite of his conciliatory 
policy and his public exhortations 2• 
Touching the different buildings mentioned in the present inscription, we 
see that the Vata-da-geya '(circular relic-house}, which is most.probably identical 
with the Vata,-geya mentioned in the Hata-da-ge 3 and Galpota records, was built 
under the supervision of General Lak-vijaya-sin.gu Tavuru-navan 
i and that 
it received the name Ratana-giri. 
The Upakara-caitya 
(subsidiary shrine), 
mentioned in line 24, is also referred to in the Galpota inscription (C, line 2), 
where it is stated that Nissanka-Malla had it built adjoining the Mahavihara 
(of Po!onnaruva), but we are not sure as to the exact situation of this monastery. 
Possibly the group of ruins in the J etavanarama area ti-iay be identified with it, 
and the U pakara-caitya may accordingly be · one of the ruined dagabas close 
by, for example, the so-called Xiri-vehera. 
Lines 34-37 give the names of cities where Nissanka-Malla is stated to 
have established alms-halls. 
Some of the.m are not mentioned in any of his

p. 13), but the statement in the Pujiival(ya that Nissailka-Malla caused a Tooth-Relic Temple 
(evidently the present one) to be constructed of stone in sixty Sinhalese hours (da{adii-~a/uyehi 
Jaz7amaya dafadii-geya sii/a-piiyakin karavii) makes it possible to ascribe the origin of the name 
to this tradition. 
Accordingly hii/a-dii-gi may be paraphrased by lzli/a piiyakin karana-lada dii-geya, 
'relic-house built in sixty hours'.

Finally 
we come to the Priti-di,naka-ma:Q.4apa. 
We are told that Nissanka-Malla 
had it built and-made its premises a sanctuary in order that he might rest there 
in bliss, 'imparting the gift of religious doctrine (dharma-dana) which is the 
noblest of all gifts' and also hear the joyous shouts of sadhu and the like 
from the people who had received alms from him. 
The location of this ma1Jefaja or pavilion is quite easy, for a flight of 
shallowly cut steps on the right leads up to a ruined building on the top 
of the rock 1• 
This is no doubt the remains of the Priti-danaka-ma1;uJapa, 
although in architectural details it does not seem to correspond with the 
Nissanka-dana-vinoda-ma1Jefapa 
built for a similar purpose 2 about a dozen 
yards to the west.

1 Mr. Bell's description of the building runs:-' 
Along the axis of thi~ rock an elongated 
rectangular building was laid out, its longest faces being 125 ft. east and west, by only 40 ft. across. 
It was certainly pillared (as stumps prove) at its northern end, and in all probability divided into 
a range of rooms, about 30 ft. wide, in a straight line along their west face throughout. 
Mo.rtice holes 
for pillars, and a "set" for wall foundation, show the southern termination. 
A gangway seems to 
have run outside the building; fer there is a bare groove in the rock, and inside it parts of the thick 
vertical pebble and lime concrete facing of the walls remain. 
Outhouses probably occupied the eastern slopes of the rock, which are the widest. 
A flight of some twenty-five shallow steps cut in the rock leads down direct west.'-A.

II (1186-n87 
A.n.) 
T
HIS slab stands near the ancient irrigation canal at Polonnaruva. 
Both 
sides of it are smoothed so as to receive the inscription between ruled 
lines; .two inches apart. 
Side A has 3 7 lines, covering an area of S ft. 8 in. by 
1 ft. 7 in.: side B, 28 lines, occupying 4 ft. 5 in. by I ft. 7 in. of the surface. 
With the exception of a few words and letters here and there, lines 3 to 7 of 
side A and the whole of side B are illegible. So at least it appears from the two 
inked estampages before me 1• 
The letters, which vary in size from ¾ to 1f in., agree in type with the 
alphabet of the latter half of the · twelfth century A. n. 
The style of the 
:.::. ~guage too points to the. same period. 
After the usual auspicious word svasti and a Sanskrit verse of which only 
the first line is partially legible, the record goes on to state that Vijaya, the 
eldest son of Sirhha-Bahu of the Kaliriga-Cakravarti dynasty came over to 
.. 
Ceylon, defeated the Yak~s, and became king; that a descendant of his was 
Parakrama-Bahu, 
who brought the Island of Lanka under one canopy of 
dominion ; and that this king, desiring the continuation of his dynasty, invited 
his sister's son (bana) over from Sirhhapura, invested 1 him with royal dignity, 
and in course of time died. 
The nephew was thereafter duly anointed king 
Vijaya-Bahu, but the day after his accession to the throne some treacherous 
m101sters rose against him. 
A chieftain named Vijayayan-tan-navan 
2, 
however, protected the king and, quelling the reb::!llion, restored peace to the 
country. 
In recognition of these distinguished services, king Vijaya-Bahu 
granted him heritable lands with certain privileges described on side B, 
lines 1 to 22, and ending with the usual clause to the effect that the regulations 
so enacted should be preserved. 
The remaining six lines contain an illegible 
Sanskrit stanza in Tamil character of the type in use during the twelfth 
century A. D. 
Such are the contents of the present inscription. 
The historical facts

therein alluded to not only corroborate the account in the Mahii:va1izsa but also 
throw additional light on the short reign of that unhappy monarch Vijaya-
Bahu II (II86-II87 
A. n.). \Ve are now absolutely certain that he was a son 
of a ~ister 1 of Parakrama-Bahu 
I ; and, as is shown in the genealogical table 
facing p. 59 above, this sister could be no other than Bhaddavati, the spouse~ 
of king Gaja-Bahu II (r 132-1153 A.D.), for Parakrama-Bahu had only two other 
sisters who were married to his hostile cousin MaQabharai;ia, son of Siri Vallabha. 
Their issues were Siri Vallabha and Kitti-Siri-Megha, and they all belonged to 
the party which opposed the political ascendancy of the Kalinga dynasty. 
It is 
true, however, that in the course of the war both these princes were taken 
captive 3 and were brought before Parakrama-Bahu, but nothing is known as to 
their fate and we have no grounds to presume that Parakrama-Bahu 
took pity 
on them and adopted one of them as his heir. 
It is also true that there 
is the statement of certain Buddhist monks in Mv. lxx. 333 that Gaja-Bahu II 
had neither a son nor any brothers, but this may mean, judging from the 
circumstances under which the statement 
was made, that he had no son or 
brother near him at the time to continue the war and eventually to succeed 
him on the throne. 
In the absence of any reference to a fourth sister of 
Parakrama-Bahu 
I, it is probable that his bana or nephew was Bhaddavati's 
son either by Gajil-Bahu II or by a second marriage, unless, of course, the word 
bana is applied loosely, as is often done, to indicate a more distant relative. 
As to 
where the nephew was when Parakrama-Bahu sent for him, the chronicles are silent. 
The inscription alone tells us quite definitely that he was then living in Sirhhapura, 
the capital of Kalinga. 
We must, therefore, assume that when war broke out 
between Gaja-Bahu II and Parakrama-Bahu I, Bhaddavati, queen of the former 
and sister of the latter, flecl to India with her son for safety as many a royal 
personage had done so before. 
Some years later the Buddhist monks brought 
about a reconciliation 4 between the two monarchs. 
This, and the continuation 
of the war with MaQabharaQa may have paved the way for Parakrama-Bahu to 
look on Bhaddavati' s son with favour. 
So, when he found towards the close of 
his reign that he was still childless and the question of a successor had to be 
settled, he rightly chose this prince in preference to the sons of his other sisters 
by MaQabharaQa. 
That there was much opposition to this election is clear both 
from the insurrection that took place on the day after the accession of this

IMBULA-GALA 
(' Gunner Quoin' 
Hill), called in the present record 
Dum.bula-gala, is a range of hills about ten miles to the south-east of 
Po}onnaruva or sixty miles from Anuradhapura in the same direction. 
The Archaeological Commissioner (Mr. H. C. P. Bell) who made a thorough 
exploration of the whole locality in September 1897, tells us that 'at the back 
the cliff towers slightly concave (recalling the east face of Sigiriya, but steeper) 
with many bambara wada (rock-bee hives) hanging hundreds of feet up. 
Further 
east the range rises still higher with two more rocky scarps well marked.

Directly behind Ku<;la U}pota is a slight dip in the range (degala) at no mean 
height. 
North-west by north, nestling high near the summit, can be seen some 
caves with white piastered walls, like the Sigiriya "gallery''. 
At the east end of 
Dimbula-gala lies Kosgaha U}pota, another Vadda hamlet; and round opposite 
its west face Mannampitiya, the largest and most thriving village in Taman-
ka<;luwa, two miles this side of the Mahavali-ganga across the Mahagantota ferry 
. . . . . . . . All the west, north-westerly side of Dimbula-gala is known as Mara-· 
ridiya from the ancient road which passed round its base to Mannampitiya. 
The highest point is immediately west of the dip and above the caves. 
Thence 
the hill gradualli falls away round to northwards with two rocky buffs breaking 
the outline. 
The approach to the caves is along a spur and very gradual until 
nearing the cliff under which the caves lie. 
These were natural caverns in the 
scarp near its summit. 
Cave No. I is the best preserved: 
its plastered walls 
are nearly perfect, and paintings which adorned them may be faintly traced. 
This cave has an arched doorway and another entrance. 
High up on the over-
hanging rock beyond the reach of ladder is an inscription of very large letters. 
Passing to the left a rock pool of clearest water, a gradual rise by a ledge, two 
to three feet only in width, leads towards the second cave, ~o. 3, thirty yards or 
more east. 
A few yards' crawl along the ledge, a dip through a natural rock 
tunnel, more creeping across a further ledge equally narrow, then descent to a 
broader passage, culminates in a second tunnel. This emerges on to cave No. 2. 
A fine view is obtained of the Kandyan hills from this cave. 
It is larger than 
No. I, and was centuries ago a gal vihare. 
The rock floor being wider here 
than at any other point, provided a fair-sized natural terrace in front, 
Portions 
of the walls still stand, and there are remains of drawings mostly in black and 
white. 
On the rock roof are two inscriptions-the 
older in a few cave letters, the 
second dated in the twenty-seventh year of" Jaya Bahu" (Wijaya Bahu I, 1065-
1 I 20 A. n.). This latter record of seven lines is cut on a smooth raised panel, and 
is of great interest. 
It proves the occupation in the eleventh century by monks, 
for whom the caves were prepared by Queen Sundari, wife of Wikrama Bahu I 
1I21-1142 
A. D.) and mother of Gaja Bahu I, the cousin and chief rival of 
Parakrama Bahu the Great.' 
Such is Mr. Bell's lucid description of the locality. 
The inscription with 
which we are concerned here is that engraved on the raised panel between ruled 
lines two inches apart in Sinhalese characters of the twelfth century A.D., varying

The contents 
tell 
us that Sundara-Maha-devi,

2• 
It is clear from these historical references that the inscription belongs neither 
to Vijaya-Bahu I nor to his brother Jaya-Bahu I, but to Sundara-Maha-devi. 
It is the only record by her so far known to us, and was set up in her capacity as 
the chief queen of Vikrama-Bahu I ( 1 I I 1-1132 A. o.)3. That this view must 
be correct we see first from the form of the script and the phraseology which 
debar us from giving the inscription a date later than the third quarter of the 
twelfth century A.D., secondly from the reference to Gaja-Bahu II (1132-1153 A.D.) 
by the title deva which suggests that he had not yet· come to the throne, and, 
thirdly, from Sunda;a-devi's confirmation of the benefaction which she had made 
to Dema!a-paha in the reign of her father-in-law, Vijaya-Bahu I (1055-1110 A.n.). 
Her object was obvously to make in her present official position a legal record 
:>f the gift. 
It seems that as the chief queen of the reigning monarch she had 
the right to make such permanent grants to public institutions-a 
right which 
she apparently 
did not enjoy when her husband Vikrama-Bahu 
was only 
a viceroy 4 of Vijaya-Bahu I.

may be drawn to the name Sundara-Maha-devi.

OF KALYANAVAT! 
T
HIS stone was discovered between the years 1906 
and 1912 
in Bopitiya, 
·a village in Hevavissa Korale in the Central Province of Ceylon. 
As the 
facsimile (plate 30) shows, it is in two fragments. 
The first piece is the top 
portion of a slab about 2\ ft. wide. 
It contains the first six lines of the inscrip-
tion. 
The second piece evidently belongs to the lower end, as we see on it the 
words ht'ra sanda, 'sun and moon', which usually occur at the end of a grant. 
The letters, measuring 1½ 
to 2½ inches in size, are boldly engraved between 
ruled lines three inches apart. 
Their type is practically the same as that of 
other records of the last quarter of the twelfth and the first of the thirteenth 
century A. D. 
Of the inscriptions of Nissanka-Malla's 
queen, Kalyai;iavati, who, like 
Lilavati, bore the title Abha Salamevan, only two are so far known. 
The first 
is the one on the pavement of Ruvanvali dagaba 1 at Anuradhapura, dated in 
her second regnal year, and the second is the present record. 
Though we have 
here only a fragment of the latter, yet what little information its contents give 
throws some light on the final events of her reign. 
As stated in the article 
No. 14 of Volu~e I on the slab-inscription of Lilavati, nothing is known 
regarding _the fate of Sahasa-Malla whom Lag-Vijaya-singu Abona or Ayasmanta 
installed on the throne on Wednesday August 23, 
1200 
A.D., and deposed after 
he had reigned two years, which would be up to September 
I 202. 
Thereafter 
the latter administered the government for six years through Queen Kalya.Q.avati 
of the present record, and for one year subsequently by placing on the throne 
a three-months-old prince named Dhammasoka. 
Then a governor called Ani-
kanga, with a large army from the Cola country, invaded the Island, put both 
Ayasmanta and Dhammasoka to death, and took up the reins of government. 
The chronicles are silent as to what became of Kalyaq.avafi. T~at she disappeared 
from the scene is certain. 
Otherwise Ayasmanta, her champion, would surely 
not have placed somebody else on the throne. 
The mystery is to some extent 
cleared up by the present record. 
The Tamil insurrection ~hich it speaks of, is 
probably Anikariga's invasion about I 208 
A. D. 
The destruction of Kalyaq.a-
vati's stronghold by the Tamils might be interpreted as the defeat of Ayasmanta 
in a battle, when Kalya.Qavati had to seek safety in flight across the river Mahavali-

ganga into the mountainous districts of Kandy.

But the following arguments may be urged in support 
of the theory that these names refer to one and the same person :-
(a) Ayasmanta (Skt. ayufmat, Sinh. abo) is not a proper name. 
It is an 
honorific title applied to Buddhist monks and elderly persons in high positions. 
At the time of Queen KalyaQavati { 1202-1208 
A. D.) Lag-Vijayasillgu Kit Senevi 
might have been popularly spoken of as Senevi Abo-nava1i, in Pali Ayasmanta-
camupatt', 'the venerable general', owing to his seniority in age and rank, just as 
a king might be referred to by a p~pular title such as mahallaka-rajii {Sinh. 
mahalu raja), 'the old king', more than by his proper name. 
(b) The close similarity of the two names Lag Vijayasingu Kit Senevi and 
Lag Vi:fa;1as£ngu Senevi .Abo-navan, the last word being only an honorific. 
(c} The contemporaneity of the bearers of these names and the similarity 
of the role they played in politics within a period of only twelve years.

N uvara Eliya District. 
The inscribed stone shown in the accompanying 
facsimile (plate 30) was found in this village between the years 1906 and 1912 2, 
but no details are available as to its discovery. 
The abrupt ending of the 
inscription as well as the sun and moon emblems carved above it show that the 
stone is only the top fragment of a pillar about 13½ inches square. The letters, 
varying from one to two inches in size, are incised as usual between ruled lines 
two inches apart. 
Their type is the same as that of Lilavati's slab-inscription 
forming No. 14 of the first volume of the present work, though the letters m and 
r show a shade more modern.

palaeographic considerations to be I 2 I I A,D., when Parakkama of the Ka1anagara

government for seven months until deposed by the PaQ.<;lyan King Parakkama.

Abha Salamevan, and the present record refers to her as belonging to the Solar 
race.

In the foregoing. notes I have, I think, met all the important points raised 
by Mr. Bell in respect of the record under discussion, with the exception of the 
question as to its date. 
I have already admitted that Mr. Bell's eye-copy and the photographic 
facsimile of the inscription distinctly give the date as the twenty-seventh year 
(after the coronation) of Jaya-Bahu 
I. 
Nevertheless, 
the record belongs to 
Queen Sundara-mahadevi 
and not to the reign of Jaya-Bahu as Mr. Bell 
contends, for the simple reason that J aya-Bahu was no longer living at the 
time when the inscription was indited. 
This anomaly of dating from the coronation of a deceased king, the first 
of its kind yet known in Sinhalese chronology, requires explanation, as it raises 
the important question of the use of the coronation of deceased kings in dating 
records 1• 
That this is true in the case of J aya-Bahu I is obvious from the 
following facts :-
Vijaya-Bahu I and his successor Jaya-Bahu I being uterine brothers, it is 
not altogether unreasonable to suppose that the difference of age between them 
was not more than fifteen years. 
Vijaya-Bahu I died after keeping his seventy-
third birthday festivities 2, that is to say, he died in his seventy-fourth year. 
Jaya-Bahu I succeeded him immediately. 
So Jaya-Bahu's age at the time of 
his coronation mtr.St have been at least fifty-nine. 
Now a Tamil 
pillar-
inscription 3 in Po!onnaruva is dated in the thirty-eighth 
year of Jaya-Bahu 
who is correctly identified with Jaya-Bahu I of our inscription. 
Thus, if this 
King was alive at the time, he would have been over ninety-seven years of age. 
He would also have been over eighty-six years of age when our record was 
composed. 
Such longevity is not very probable. 
The shorter the difference 
of age between the two brothers, the stronger becomes my argument 
on 
this point. 
Moreover, if we follow the sequence of events as narrated in the Jf,,fahii-
vamsa (eh. lxi and lxii), we are bound to come to the conclusion that Jaya-
Bahu's death took place in RohaQ.a during the _lifetime of Vikkama-Bahu 
(lxii, 1-2) and long before the birth of Parakkama-Bahu I, whom Vikkama-Bahu 
1 Dr. Fotheringham, a well-known authority on dates, tells me that Papyrus B in Aramaic papyri 
discovered at Asman, edited by Sayce and Cowley (1906), is dated in the twenty-first year of Xerxes, 
though it really belongs to a time when Xerxes was dead and Artaxerxes had been proclaimed King. 
The exact date of the papyrus is 2nd January, 464 B.c. 
9 PoJonnaruva Tamil slab-inscription (A.S.C., Annual Report, 1911-1912).

offered to adopt as his successor (Mv., lxii, 52-62). 
Vikkama-Bahu died in 
the twenty-second year of his Po1onnaruva rule and was succeeded by his son 
Gaja-Bahu II, who held the sceptre for twenty-two years (Mv., lxiii, 18-19, 
and lxxi, 1-5. 
Thus the information we have regarding the period that 
elapsed between the death of Vijaya-Bahu I and that of Gaja-Bahu II may be 
expressed as follows :-
(a) The length of Jaya-Bahu's rule at PoJonnaruva up to 
his enforced retirement to Roha9a on Vikkama-
Bahu's wresting the sceptre from him . 
. =X 
(b) Vikkama-Bahu's PoJonnaruva rule 
. = 21 years 
(c) His son Gaja-Bahu's rule . 
. = 22 years 
(")_ The Tamil pillar-inscription makes the fifteenth year 
of Gaja-Bahu = the thirty-eighth year of J aya-
Bahu. 
If we reduce this to an equation we get 
x+21+15=38 
x = 2 years. 
This result practically agrees witli the Sinhalese chronicles. 
Jaya-Bahu I 
was not c11lowed to rule long at Po!onnaruva. 
Vikkama-Bahu ousted him in his 
third year, as confirmed by the three years' reign allotted to him in the Raja-
valiya. But the most important bit of information which throws light on the 
Jaya-Bahu riddle is to be found in the Pujavali'ya. It is stated there that he 
reigned for fourteen years. 
I take this to mean that he ruled about two years 
in Polonnaruva and lived for about twelve years in retirement as de jure King 
of Ceylon, exactly agreeing with what one can gather from th~ account in the 
111ahavainsa as stated above. 
Jaya-Bahu's death must, therefore, have taken 
place in the thirteenth year of Vikkama-Bahu's reign and he was at the time 
about seventy-three years old. 
Thus the date thirty-eight years of Jaya-Bahu 
in the Tamil inscription is composed of fourteen years (2 + 12) of.his lifetime and 
twenty-four years after his death. 
Similarly, our Dimbulagala inscription, dated 
in the twenty-seventh year after his coronation, was actually incised in the 
thirteenth (expired) year after his death, which, according to the Makavamsa, 
would also be the fourth year after the death of Vikkama-Bahu or the fourth

reckoned from the coronation of the deceased monarch Jaya-Bahu I, two reasons 
might be urged. 
First, his successors Vikkama-Bahu and Gaja-Bahu were not 
crowned, and so the documents had to be dated from the last crowned king, in 
conformity perhaps with general usage in such matters. 
Secondly, Vikkama-
Bahu, ~s Mr. Bell has already pointed out, was no friend of the Buddhist 
church. 
His 'son, Gaja-Bahu, too, was not thought of highly (Mv., lxii, 
58- 59), nor was he at any time firmly established on the throne 1, whereas 
Jaya-Bahu was a monarch fully recognized and favoured by the priesthood. 
In these circumstances, it was quite natural and reasonable on the part of 
Sundara-mahadevi, the queen-dowager, tt> allow the composer of the inscription 
to follow the usual form of expression and make mention of her late royal 
spouse Vikkama-Bahu I and her royal son Gaja-Bahu II (then ruling at Polon-
naruva) and yet to have the record dated from the coronation of Jaya-Bahu 
either by way of pleasing the pious monks then residing at Dimbulagala 
or at their special request, or to make the grant perfect in the eye of the law.

(Lines 1-6]. 
His Majesty, King Siri San.gabo Vijaya-Bahu 1, was born 2 
unto the great King Abba Salamevan 
3, the K~atriya Lord 4 descended from 
the Royal line oft.he Okkaka dynasty, [a branch] of the Solar race 5, which, 
abounding in a multitude of benignant, boundless and transcendental virtues 6, 
has caused other K~atriya dynasties of the whole of J ambudvipa (India) to 
render it homage 7• 
(He was born] in the womb of Queen 8 (Dev Gon) of 
equal birth and descent 9• 
[Lines 6-10] 
After enjoying the dignities of Governor and Chief Governor, 
he,· in due course, became King, and was anointed on his head, resplendent with 
the bejewelled crown, with the unction of world supremacy. 
He is (thus] like 
unto a tilaka mark (of adornment) to the lineage of great lords 10 of the soil of 
Lanka, anointing the heads of other Kings with the effulgence of the nails 
of his feet. 
[Lines 10-15] 
He has surpassed 11 the Sun in the majesty inherent in 
him, Mahesvara (Siva) in prowess, Vi~9u in haughty spirit, the Chief of the 
Gods (Indra) 
in kingly state, the· Lord of riches (Kuvera) in inexhaustible 12 
wealth, Kitisuru 13 in (bestowing) happiness to living beings, the Preceptor 
of the Gods (Brhaspati) in the fertility of his wisdom, the Moon in gentleness,

day of the waxing moon, (His Majesty) made offerings of various adornments 
studded with beautiful gems of seven kinds to the Sacred Footprint 1 impressed 
on the summit of Samanola rock (Adam's Peak) which sustained the Sacred 
lotus-like feet of the four Buddhas that attained Buddhahood in the present 
cycle, namely, Kakusandha, KoQagamana, Kassapa, and Gotama. 
He raised 
also various canopies, flags and banners made of silk cloth (over the footprint) 
and, anointing it with the four kinds of unguents, he decked it with his own 
bejewelled crown. 
[Lines 28-38] 
Thereafter, 
he instituted 
the maintenance 
of repairs, 
offerings, paintings, lighting of lamps on Samanola rock (Adam's Peak) which 
bears the sacred footprint (of the Buddha) ; and for providing the great 
commtinity of Buddhist monks who arrive from the four quarters to worship 
the (foot-)relic here, with suitable food and other necessary things, and also for 
keeping up the alms given to those other travel-worn pilgrims who come 
together to worship the relic, he had almonries (dana-sala) established in his 
name, one at each of the last five gows of Raja-raia road 2 and endowed them 
with means for almsgiving. 
He had a terrace c.onstructed below the terrace 
where the sacred footprint is, and [thus gave facility] for Jow caste people to 
worship the relic of the Sage 3• 
He had the first terrace enclosed by a great 
wall with two gateways at the two roads [leading in and out], which are 
fitted with locks and keys. 
[Thus] did he give those worthy of his protection 
facility to worship the relic of the Sage. 
He had a net also put over· the 
sacred footprint, and in the neighbourhood all round it he caused the formation 
of paddy fields. 
[Lines 38-50] 
He moreover made [ a partition of] Vilba and dedicated 
(to the sacred footprint) all the [following] properties (situated} therein, namely, 
one garden• of areca-nut trees in Kelagamuva, one ko/avaH in Tiniyagal, one 
ko/avali in Sorago9a, one ko/avali in Liyava1a, one ko/avali in the forest of 
Bad ulla, the areca-nuts of the ko/avalla at the U c;lu-ho ( upper stream), as well as

HOUGH 
kings of old Ceylon, like those of Southern India, have left 
behind a very large number of inscriptions recording .their charitable acts, 
yet, with the exception of a few of a comparatively late period, all followed 
the ancient method of dating by regnal years of kings. 
This, however, does 
not help us much in the task of arranging the chronology of Ceylon kings. 
So the present record of Sahasa-Malla with its definite date in the Buddha-var~a, 
the earliest yet come to light, is of great historical interest. 
It was found more than half a century ago incised on a quadrangular slab 
(about 6r X 2¾) standing upright at a spot north of the Hatadage on the present 
footpath to Rankot-vehera in Polonnaruva. 
Both . the sides of the stone are 
made smooth and are ruled horizontally with lines two inches apart to receive 
between them the inscription boldly engraved in 69 lines (32 on side A and 37 
on side B). 
The type of the ak~aras agrees with that of the alpnabet · of the twelfth 
and thirteenth centuries. 
There is as usual no noticeable difference between 
the r vowel sign and ra when affixed to a consonant. 
The medial long a vowel 
sign (alapilla) is attached to the lower end of I, ~. as in the records of this period, 
though in a few inscriptions we find it detached as 61(3:> in side B, line 3. The 
v£sarga is indicated by the usual vertical stroke convexed to the left ( c ), some· 
times by double curves ~ as in nrpa!z 
{side B, line 37). 
The orthography is correct with few exceptions such as sewhich is sometimes 
written se, the doubling of consonants in conjunction with a preceding r so common 
in manuscripts and, in one instance only, the unnecessary use of the virama in 
consonantal groups of Sanskrit and Pali words, instead of the combined letters, 
e.g. vighna (B, line 5). 
The grammar also is satisfactory, although we should prefer the addition 
of vu after urehi-da (A, lines 7-8) and of the genitive suffix ge after mahadevzn-
vahanse (A, line 8). 
The language is Sanskritic Sinhalese and agrees in style with tha:t of the 
inscriptions of Nissanka-Malla. 
The first five lines of side A and the last five 
lines of side B contain two Sanskrit stanzas in sardulavikrzrjita metre separated 
from the Sinhalese text by a fish emblem as shown in the facsimile.

[VOL. II 
The date given in the inscription is r 743 years, 3 months and 2 7 days of 
the Buddhavar!ja, Wednesday\ the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the lunar 
month of Binera (Bhadrapada, Aug.-Sept.). 
It is not that of the record itself or 
of the grant, but that of the anointment of Sahasa-Malla as king of Ceylon and, 
as already stated, it is the earliest known instance of the use of the Buddhist 
era in a public document. 
Dr. Fleet, in his article on this subject 2, says that 
the year 1743 treated as the completed year in_ accordance with the general 
practice, takes us, for the given month, to r 200 A. D. or 1201 according as it_ is 
counted from an initial point in 544 or in 543 B. c. The given details, Bhadra-
pada sukla 12, Wednesday are correct for Wednesday, 23rd August, 1200 
A. D. 
So we have the date of the anointment of Sahasa-Malla (alias Siri Saiigabo 
Kalinga Vijaya-Bahu) as a definitely fixed point in the later chronology. 
Further, this result shows that when the reckoning was set going, it was 
made to run from an initial point in 544 B. c. (not 543). As to how far back 
this reckoning of the Buddha-var~a from 544 B. c. was in vogue in preference 
to, or rather in ignorance of, the earlier one reckoned from 483 B. c., the reader 
is referred to pages 208-209 above where the question has been threshed out 
to some extent. 
The contents of the record tell us that Siri Sa:iigabo Kalinga Vijaya-
Bahu bore the lriruda epithet Saha~a--Malla, that he was born in Sirhhapura 
as a legitimate son of Sri-Gopa of the Kalinga Cakravarti dynasty by Queen 
Loka-mabadevi, that he was a brother of Nissanka-Malla who was king of 
Ceylon before him, that after the latter's death, one Lolupala-kuJu Diittati 
Abonavan, an adhigar of Ceylon, in association with his friend and colleague 
Lolupiila-kaju Budal-navan, also an adhigar of Ceylon, determined to reinstate 
the Kali.riga dynasty on the throne and so sent a Kalinga noble calleq Malli-
karjuna, to Sirnhapura with an invitation to Sahasa-Malla to come over and take 
up the sovereignty of Ceylon, that after two years, when the two adhigars had 
completed the subjugation of their antagonists, he was raised to the throne and 
was anointed on the above-mentioned date, that in recognition of these services, 
the king raised the first adhigar to the rank of Senevirat and his mother to that 
of Lankatilaka-mahadevi 
with the decoration of the waist-band of gold and 
that. he further appointed the Senevirat called also Lak-Vijaya-Siiigu-Senevi 
.A.bona.van as his prime minister and granted him much wealth in the shape 
of pamunu lands, escorts, &c.

As regards the ministers, we see that Ayu~mat-p:rtanapati 
mentioned 
in the Sanskrit verse both at the beginning and at the end of the inscription 
is identical with Lak-Vijaya-Siiigu Senevi A..bonavan and most probably with

for it was this general that was instrumental in placing Sahasa-Malla on the 
throne and it was he who received gifts and honours for his loyal services 
to the king. 
It is true that owing to the political intrigues that w~re going 
on at the time between the contending parties at the Court, as explained above 
(pp. 101-103), Sahasa-Malla's reign did not last long. 
What happened to him 
is not stated anywhere, but we read in the Mahiivamsa, (eh. lxxx., 32-44) t~at 
after the second year of this king's reign, this Ayu~mat general, 'a bold and 
resolute man', took the power into his own hands and ruled the country

according to law ai:id justice for six years with the help of Kalyal)avati, the

J\ LUTV .AVA is a hamlet in Eppavala Korale, North Central· Province. 
J-"\. The inscribed pillar here is one of those examined by Mr. H. C. P. Bell 5 
in 1895. 
It is quadrangular and measures about 4ft. by 9~ in. square. 
The ak1:1aras, each about an inch in size, are clearly incised between ruled 
lines two inches apart. 
They cover three sides of the pillar, sides A and B con-
taining 21 lines in each, and side C 12 lines, terminating with the usual emblems of 
the sun, the moon, the crow, and the dog, one above the other in succession, as

may be seen from th~. accompanying facsimile. 
Generally speaking, the letters 
resemble the alphabet of the tenth century A, D. 
A comparison, however, of the 
aksaras z', ka, ma, ya, and ra in the present record with those in the pillar-
inscriptions of Iripinniyava 1 Rambava, Kirigallava, and Noccipotana, ascribed 
to Udaya I (circa 952-963 A.D.) will make it obvious that palaeographically our 
inscription belongs to a date later than these. 
The same reasons compel us to 
consider our record to be even later than the pillar-inscriptions at Timbirivava 
2 
and Na.Kama 2 of the first and the seventh year respectively of Kassa pa IV 
(circa 963-980 A.D.). On the other hand, the script both of Kukurumahan-
damana 2 pillar of the eleventh year of Kassapa IV and of the Mac;lirigiriya 
pillar of the third year of Kassapa V (cz'rca 980-990 A.n.) resembles that of the 
present record in every respect. 
Further, at page 9 above, we have pointed out that many of the ninth- and 
tenth-century kings, such as Sena I and his successors down to Dappula V, 
appear to have adopted the biruda titles Salamevan and Siri Sangbo alternately. 
Accordingly Sena II was a Siri Sangbo, his successor Udaya I, a Salamevan, 
and the next king, Kassapa IV, a Siri Sangbo. 
The king mentioned in our 
record of about the same period was also a Siri Sa11gbo. This fact makes us 
identify him either with Sena II or Kassapa IV. 
The form of script, as stated 
before, is decidedly against the former identification, while the · regnal year, if 
taken as the twentieth, supports it, for Sena I I was the only king about this time 
who held the sceptre for more than twenty years. 
If, however, we accept the 
alternative reading pas vanne, 'fifth year', as the correct one instead of vas 
vanne3, there will be no difficulty in classing the record as one of Kassapa IV. 
There are two dates in our inscription, both in the same month of U nd-vap 
and in the same regnal year. 
The first is ava viseni davas (A, lines 5-6), ' the 
fifth day of the waning moon', and is apparently the day on which the aecree 
was passed by the King in Council. 
The second is pun mashi dasa pak davas 
{C, lines 5-6) 'the tenth day of the bright half of the month'. 
It is the date on 
which the attatpi perahara or the Council Warrant was proclaimed. 
But both 
these dates being in one and the same month of U nd-vap and if the month 
was an amiinta Und-vap, the second date referring to a subsequent event should 
also be in the apara pak~a like the first date, otherwise it would fall in amanta 
Durutu, the montli after Und-vap. 
We are, therefore, compelled .to think

that the month in question was a pun;imanta U nd-vap, which 1s calculated to

Owing to the illegibility of certain words in the text, we are unable to say 
what the exact purport of the Council Warrant 
is. 
Th~ readable portion 
enumerates certain properties in Mahademeti-kuliya, which were at the time 
under the management of one Tin<;li Kitu, but whet_her they were gifted to this 
man or whether he only received certain privileges in connexion therewith, we 
are unable to gather from the present imperfect text. 
The two officials who carried out the order of the King in Council were 
(a) Mekappar Mahanavagam-ka9ayim 
Kela Mihindim of the family of Mangul-
rad Senu and (b) :irul).9asala 2 Viset-devu 
of the family of Maha.le Kasbi 
Raksamai;i.an. Neither of them is mentioned in any of the records yet known to 
us, but Kur:ic;lasala Viset-devu may have been closely related to Kui;i.9asala Kit 
of the Mac;liligiri pillar of Kassapa V and to Kur:i<;lasala Singim of the Atavfra-
gollava pillar of Dappula V and also to Kavasilar.ig Gavayim qf Kirigallava pillar 
of U daya I, because they were kinsmen of the Chief Secretary Kasha Raksamar:ian. 
The language of our record is similar in style to. that employed in other 
pillar-inscriptions of the tenth and eleventh centuries. There are, however, a few 
agricultural terms that need elucidation. 
They are (a) hevi/iya probably for 
hovi/iya, modern ovi/iya, possibly a derivative of Skt. frotas (P. sota, Pkt. soa) + 
pr#ha (or*Pr#hika, P.and Pkt.pitthz), 'the lowland bya riverside'; (b) kariirtasa 
or kiiriirsa probably land under certain form of tenure, (c) kiri, pa, and massa. 
These are no doubt names of measures of capacity. 
When applied to land 
measure they mean the extent of land which they will normally cover in sowing. 
Kiri is the same as kz'riya or karzsa 3 and is equivalent to four amu~izt (P. amma~za). 
Pa or paya (Skt'. pada) is a quarter of a kiri, i.e. an amzt~za4, while a massa, a term 
known to us only as the name of a coin 5 , seems from the context to indicate that it 
is equal to a quarter of a pa in which case it is another name for a paya!a or pataa.

T
H1S inscription was discovered in July 1921 at a spot' about 92 feet east 
of o mile 60 chains on the Po)onnaruva section of the railway trace to 
Batticaloe' in or near the village called Anaulundava, north of Polonnaruva 1• 
It consists of three lines of writing engraved between ruled lines 1 ½ in. 
apart and covering an area of only 4½ in. by 3 ft. s½ 
in. at the upper end of 
the prepared surface of a stone slab measuring 6 ft. 10 in. x 3 ft. s½ x 10 in. The 
top part is obviously intended to remain above ground ,and is, therefore, 
ornamented with ogee moulding on its sides. 
The script is Sinhalese, the size of each letter being about 1¾ in. on 
the average. 
The type is that of the alphabet of the twelfth and thirteenth 
centuries. 
As to the language, we cannot say that it is wholly Sanskrit owing to the 
total illegibility of the third line, but what is readable consists only of a number 
of high sounding titles of honour in Sanskrit. 
It will be seen from the notes 
following the translation tha~ these titles are practically identical with those 
applied to certain members of a guild of merchants called Vira-Ba:i;iaiiju or 
Vira-Valaiijiyar 
2 who are referred to as prominent donors in several of the 
Kanarese inscriptions 
of the twelfth century A. D., for example those from 
Kolhapur, Miraj, and Mamdapiir. 
I am indebted to Dr .. Barnett not only for 
drawing my attention to the similarity of the titles but also for kindly giving 
me all the references to the Vira-Va}afijiyar.

HE so-called 'Pot-Gul Vehera' is the central shrine of a group of ruined 
buildings erected on raised sites within a quadrangular mound once· held 
up by a brick rampart faced with elephant head decorations. 
It lies about 
a mile to the south of the ancient city of PoJonnaruva, not far from the southern 
end of the Topa-vava bund 1. In his annual report for 1906 (pp. 10-17), the 
late Archaeological Commissioner (Mr. H. C. P. Bell) has given a detailed and 
exhaustive description, as well as a plan, of the whole site. 
In order to make 
the contents of the present inscription more intelligible to our readers, we give 
here a reproduction of the plan II and quote the following passages ·from his 
account:-
' The sole means of access to the raised site upon which stand the structure, 
now styled "Pot-gul Vehera", and its annexes was up a perron stairway, with 
plain faced wing walls, footP.d by rough pavement.' 
'On mounting to the precincts of the shrines it is seen that the temenos 
was slightly oblong, measuring 130 ft. from east to·west by 112 ft. across north 
and south.. It oose 7 ft. above the level of the inner quadrangre, which contains 
the pirz'ven lying below.' 
'Within the sacred temenos the same symmetry is again noticeable as in 
· the arrangement of the flanking pi'riven.' 
' Here are situated a central shrine "supported" by four diminutive stupas 
at each corner of the quadrangular peribole, following the exact disposition of 
those quincunx coteries of a vihare and its four appurtenant pz'riven s_o familiar 
amid the ruins at Anuradhapura.' 
' The four small ruined dagabas are of one size, 18 ft in diameter, and were 
probably mere cenotaphs, added to appropriately balance, and set off, the 
important shrine located in the middle of the temenos.' 
'And that shrine, unidentified but obviously mistermed " Pot-gul Vehera" 
was well worthy of such special honour. 
For this structure is perhaps unique in 
the ancient Buddhist architecture of Ceylon. 
Certainly no other ruin at all like 
it has been yet discovered in the Island.'

T
HE present inscription was, we believe, brought to public notice for the 
first time by Mr. H. C. P. Bell in his Annual Report of the Ceylon 
Archaeological Survey for 1903 (p. 11). His words are: 'To the west of Vihare 
No. 2 1, close to its basement is lying prone a fine slab of granite (9ft. 6 in. 
by 2 ft. 9 in.), on which are cut, inside beaded framing, forty-four lines of writing 
in Tamil and Grantha characters, besides five more lines at the head. Below are 
carved_ a pair of vases in messo relievo. But this inscription has no connection 
whatever with the present vihare.' 
The appendix to this report contains 
a provisional translatio9 
of the record by Mudaliyar 
R. C. Kailasa PiHai 
with Mr. Bell's historical introduction. 
His Annual Report for 1911-1912 
(appendix, E), furnishes us with a complete text and an improved translation 
with explanatory notes contributed by Rao Sahib H. Krish9a Sastri Avarga}. 
We have, moreover, before us two fairly good ink-estampages supplied by the 
Archaeological Commissioner (Mr. Hocart), and a photographic plate published 
in Mr. Bell's report. 
These form the material utilized in the preparation of the 
present edition and translation of the record which has now been framed with 
cement and placed in situ near vihara No. 1 in Polonnaruva Quadrangle. 
As Mr. Bell says, the inscription consists of forty-nine lines clearly incised 
between ruled lines, two inches apart, and covering an area of 2 ft. 9 in. by 8 ft. 
of the smoothed surface of the slab. 
Its characters are one to two inches in 
size each, and belong to a mixed alphabet of a period between the tenth and 
the fourteenth centuries A. D.

easy reference and for the benefit of Ceylon students, will show t?e form of 
character and the particular alphabet to which each letter belongs; T. being the 
abbreviation for Tamil, G. for Grantha, and S. for Sinhalese.

mixed nature of the script we are obliged to adopt a slight modification in the

in the future.

The types shown in the foregoing list are, it is true, not unknown to 
South-Indian inscriptions. 
The virama is represented by a short vertical stroke 
over the letters as in the Tamil portion of the Ko.ram Pallava grant 1 and in 
the pillar inscription of Rajasirhha-varme~vara 
shrine 2, where the later sign, 
the pu/(i or the dot over the consonant, also occurs five times. 
Here the 
vertical virama has a close resemblance to the initial r in 1igatures, which in 
Indian inscriptions is shown by a wedge 3 or by an angle or curve open to the 
right. 
The medial ai is indicated by ~ and ~ : the former follows the Grantha 
form in having the two signs placed one a·bove the other, instead of one behind 
the other as in Rajaraja's Taf\.javo.r inscription 4, while the latter is probably an 
advanced form. 
We find, however, all these four varieties in South-Indian 
inscriptions from the tenth to the twelfth centuries 5, A.D. 
Attention may also 
be drawn to the close similarity between gr and gra, ita and nit, bha and ha, 
as well as between mu and /u. 
The anusvara is engraved on the right side 
of the ak~ara except in the case of the syllable sam, where the older method of 
marking it a ½ove the letter is retained. 
No distinction is shown between the 
short and long forms of e and o. 
As regards orthography, 
it is more or less a peculiarity of Tamil inscriptions 
to use indiscriminately Grantha letters side by side with those of Tamil.

I (1153-1186 A.n.) 
0 
NE of the monasteries built by Parakkama-Bahu I was the Uttararama 2 
(North Park) of Polonnaruva with its rock-cut temple, now popularly 
called Gal-vihara, its Buddhist figures and the inscription on the vertical 
face of the rock. These have been known to the public for a long time. 
Pilgrims, sightseers, and government officials, who have, from time to time, 
--visited the spot, have expre;:;sed in writing and otherwise their profound 
admiration of these ruins which bear witness to the religious enthusiasm and 
the artistic taste of the twelfth century A. D. 
A graphic description of the site appears from the pen of Mr. H. C. P. Bell, 
in his Annual Report of the Archaeological Survey for 1907. 
For the benefit 
of the readers of the Epigraphi'a Zeylanica, however, we need quote only an 
extract with a photograph 3 of the temple indicating the exact position of the 
inscription. 
Mr. Bell says: 'This rock-hewn_ shrine stands unrivalled as, in its special 
features, the most impressive antiquity par excellence to be seen in the Island 
of Ceylon, and possibly not rivalled throughout the Continent of India. 
The li11e of gigantic figures carved from the gray rock which forms their 
background, calm, immovable, majestic, amid the hush of the surrounding forest, 
gazing ever fixedly into space with the pensiveness of profound meditation, or 
wrapped in eternal slumber, must inspire in the thoughtful beholder wonder and 
admiration, mingled with an instinctive sense of silent awe. 
The irresistible charm and sublimity of the "Gal Vihare" could not but 
appeal forcibly to the few observant visitors who, for the last century, have 
chanced to view it in its peaceful wooded seclusion untouched by ·axe and 
spade. 
The limited outcrop of rock from which the " Gal Vihare" was formed lies 
about 1½ miles north of the Promontory 4 situated between T6pavewa lake, which 
once washed it, and the Citadel. 
It is less than a quarter of a mile from the 
extensive oblong site, artificially banked up, whereo11 are located " Kiri Vehera '' 
Dagaba, "J etawanarama" Vihare and other connected ruined buildings.

The galjota stretches from south-west to north-east, brqadly speaking; 
nowhere does it reach to more than 30 ft. above the level ground.;:;., 
It was the south-east face of this rock-reach, rising most abruptly before 
it trends eastwards, which was selected by the stone-masons as best adapted for 
this purpose. 
This portion of the rock, 56 yards in length, falls away gradually at each end, 
but most to north-east; 
and it was this physical conformation which doubtless 
decided the distribution of the several images. 
The tall standing figure, therefore, and the shrine pierced into the rock, 
occupy the middle, with the colossal recumbent Buddha and a gigantic sedent 
image to right and left respectively. 
The rock face had to be cut back nearly 15 ft. for the sculpturing of the 
three great images, and scooped out as much as 17 ft. to provide the cave shrine 
and its pronaos. 
The sloping rock face immediately to the right of the cave was chiselled 
smooth for a space ( 13 ft. 3 in. by 9 ft. 9 in.) to receive a long Sinhalese inscription 
in 51 lines, now much weathered by exposure. 
This record is a kathikawa [sic] 
or' ordinance for the guidance of Buddhist clergy, cut in stone by ..Parakrama 
Bahu (1164-1197 A.D.) 
1, the Great Monarch of Sinhalese history and tradition. 
To that rule/s credit is known to belong beyond question the construction 
of the "Gal Vihare ", whatever doubt may exist as to the many other shrines at 
which the bombastic Ni~~ai:ika Malla, his near successor, has showered his records. 
For the Mahdwa~zsa 2 chronicler alludes to the execution of the work with 
direct blunt brevity too definite to admit of dispute, however wanting in due 
appreciation of the grandeur of the most impressive sculptures existing in Lai:ika. 
"And this ruler of men built likewise the Uttardrdma, nigh unto the Maha 
Thupa, after that he had caused the rock that was there to be hewn out. 
And 
when he had finished all the work he caused cunning workmen to ,make three 
caves in the rock, namely the Vijjadhara Guhd (" the cave of the spirits of 
k_nowledge "), the Nisinnaja(imd

Such is the general description of the site. 
The photograph reproduced 
here shows exactly the spot where the inscription is on the rock-face between 
the central cave shrine and the recumbent figure of the Buddha. 
}twill also be seen from the accompanying (plate 37) facsimile of the record 
that its letters, 1½ 
in. to 2 in. each in size, are, as usual, engraved between ruled 
lines 2¼ in. apart, and that in type they may be assigned to a date between the 
Ambagamuva record of Vijaya-Bahu I (1058-1114 A.D.) 1, and the Polonnaruva 
slab of Vijaya-Bahu II (1186-1187 A.n.) 2• 
A comparison of the ak~aras ka, ta, 
na, ra, and ma in these inscriptions will make this apparent. 
There is hardly 
any difference between the medial' u, r, and ra. 
See, for example, the ak~aras 
pu, pra, and hr in line 9. 
There is also a tendency to avoid compound letters 
even in words borrowed from Sanskrit and Pali. 
As Muller has already stated 3, the language of our record is very much 
the :;ame as that of the Sinhalese commentaries of the beginning of the thirteenth 
century and of works such as the A mavatura, the Thupavamsa, &c. There is 
a good sprinkling of Sanskrit words, more than in the earlier inscriptions 4, but 
not so much as in the later ones 5• 
As regards the contents, the inscription may be divided into two parts: 
(a) the historical introduction (11. 1-18}, and (b) the disciplinary injunctions 
(11. 18-5 1 ), the end of each section being indicated· by a fish symbol. 
The historical material embodied in the introduction, when compared with 
the statement in the Mahavainsa 6; gives us the information that the Buddha 
died in the Sala grove of the 'Malla princes after a religious career of 45 years 
since his 'Enlightenment'. 
Thereafter, 
when 454 years had elapsed, there 
reigned in Ceylon Valagam Abha 7, and from thence for a period of 1254 years, 
the· Buddhist Church or siisana continued her course of disintegratio~ 8• 
Then 
<;ri Sanghabodhi Parakkama-Bahu I was already holdiog the reins of govern-
ment. 
No sooner had he brought the Island under his sway, than he turned 
his attention to reform and revivify the sasana which; he declared, as had 
DuHhagamal).i more than twelve and a half .centuries before, was his object m 
assuming sovereignty.

This is what is meant by the statement in line

~ringing about a reconciliation of the three nikayas, His Majesty made them

further the names and particulars of some of the Elders who took part in the 
rehearsal of the scriptures.

to the Samantapasadika.

It is to be noted that, strictly speaking, the king has no authority to issue orders

The Church has to do that, but t~e king can enforce their

According to Buddhaghosa, the reputed author of the Commentary on the 
Kathavatthu, 
one of the results of the third Rehearsal of the Buddhist Canon 
under Asoka's patronage was the production of the Kathavatthu by Moggaliputta-

arise' 2• 
We venture to suggest another compilation for the same purpose, 
namely, the Vz'naya-sarnukasa mentioned in the Calcutta-Bairai rock-inscription 
addressed by Asoka to the Sangha. 
Our reasons.for this assertion are: (a) Though we have as yet no reliable. 
material to accept as true the traditions of Asoka's actual conversion to 
Buddhism in the fourth year after his coronation, or of his building thousands 
of monasteries during the following three years, yet there is sufficient evidence 
to infer that he was in touch with Buddh_ism and was attracted by its tenets ; 
(b) After experiencing the horrors of the Kalinga \\ar, in the ninth year of his 
reign, he became a. Buddhist upasaka and seems to have studied Buddhist texts, 
notably the Dharnmapada, for it is its teachings that he has promulgated by 
means of his edicts ; namely, the principles of rnetta, karu1J,ii, and mudz'ta, in-
cluding ahz'msa and dana-all 
of which cove!'ed more or less common ground 
with the doctrines of other contemporary schools 3 ; {c) Like Parakkama-Bahu of 
our record, Asoka also paid visits to the Buddhist sangha 4 and presumably made 
himself acquainted with the Patimokkha and other Vinaya treatises; 
(d) As 
a result he may have himself noticed the existence of heresies in the Sangha, 
and, possibly at the request of the Elders of the Theriya sect, determined to 
purge the religion of its impurities ; (e) So, the Rehearsal of the Buddhist Canon 
may have taken place, for. the third or second time, in the seventeenth regnal

This is exactly what has happened in Ceylon. Whenever a pious king noticed

Of the later katika-vatas, we see in the Hatad;;i.ge wall-inscription 1 a fragment 
of the one issued by Kitti Nissanka Malla (1187-1196 A. D.). During the reign 
of Vijaya-Bahu III (drca 1227-1231 A.o.) Sangharakkhita Thera, a pupil of the 
celebrated author, Sa.riputta Thera of Polonnaruva, with the co-operation of 
another eminent Elder, Dumbulagala Medhankara, held an ecclesiastic2l court 
at which the sacred text was revised and a new code of disciplinary rules was 
promulgated. 
Thereafter 
his distinguished 
son Parakkama-Bahu 
II (1231-
1265 A.o.) had the Dambade'JJ,z' Katz'ka-vata issued by an assembly of Elders 
presided over by AraQ.yaka Medhankara 
of the Dumbulagala fraternity 11• 
In 
this, the authors have included practically the whole of the contents of Para-
kkama-Bahu's 
Gal-vihara katika-vata. 
Evidently 
taking this as a precedent, 
Valivita Pi1;c;lapatika SaraQ.ankara, when he and his collaborators 
issued a 
katika-vata under the patronage of King Kirti <;rI Rajasimha ( r 7 46~1780 A. n.), 
incorporated the contents of the DambadeQ.i-katika-vata. 
His successor Rajadhi 
Rajasimha (1780-1797 A. n.), also had a disciplinary rescript promulgated. 
More 
particulars regarding all these and a few others more or less fragmentary are 
given in the Katikavat-sangarii 
to which we are indebted for much useful 
information. 
As stated above, the present inscription has been known to the public for 
a long time. · But l'lo one published it until Dr. MUiler included an edition and 
an English translation of it in his Ancient Inscriptions in Ceylon (London, 1883). 
Since then an improved edition appeared in the Katikavat-sangarii 
(Colombo, 
1922). 
The edition given below is based on the two ink-estampages supplied by 
Mr. A. M. Hocart, the present Archaeological 
Commissioner of Ceylon. 
A 
perusal of the second part of the record and of the notes accompanying the 
translation will give the reader a fair idea of the strict character of the disciplinary 
rules and the scriptural authorities they are based on.

TRANSLATION. 
[Lines 1-4] 
Our Buddha having fulfilled the exercise of all the thirty 
pre-eminent virtues _1 over a period of four asankhyas and one hundred thousand 
cycles of years (kalpas), mounted on the dais at [the. foot] of the great Bodhi 2 
tree, which formed [as it were] the field of battle with Mara, vanquished this 
[well-nigh] irresistible Mara together with his host, and attained to the state of 
omniscience. 
Thereafter, for forty-five years he manifested himself like a great 
rain-cloud over the four continents, 3 and so, with showers of nectar-like Dhamma 4, 
he assuaged [the torments of] the living beings who were being burnt by the 
kle'ra 5 fire of many kalpa cycles old, numbering hundreds of thousands of kotis. 
Having thus accomplished all the duties of a Buddha, he psl-ssed away into the 
nirupadhi--fe~a 
6 nirvaJ_Za state in the grove of sala trees of the Malla princes in 
the neighbourhood of the city of Kusinara. 
[Lines 4-9] 
At the expiration of 454 years [from this event], there reigned 
the great King Va}agam Abha 7. 
Thereafter, 
for 1254 years the Buddhist 
Fraternity remained disintegrated, and the religion also continued its course of 
decadence. 
At this juncture, there came to the throne the mighty king of 
1 Parum (line 1) spelt also perum, P. piirami or paramz'ta. 
See Rhys Davids's Pali' Diet. for an 
explanation of this term. 
~ Mahii-bodhz'-paryaitka 'the divan of thorough enlightenment' (Millier). 
8 Namely, Uttarakuru on the north, Jambudvipa on the south, Pitrvavi'deha on the east, and 
Aparagodana on the west of the Maha Meru mountain which is supposed to stand on three other 
mountains ( Trz'ku/a) at the centre of the basin-like earth encircled by the Cakkava}a range. 
• Referring to the Sermons of the Buddha. 
5 For a Buddhistic definition of this word as applied to hereditary desires of a vicious nature, see 
Rhys Davids's Pait' IJz'ct. 
6 The state which leaves no substratum of being behind, that is to say, entirely free from rebirth. 
7 VaHa-GamaJ:).i Abhaya, 439 A.B. and 454-466 A,B. (44 and 29-17 B.c.).

senior bhikkhu, the junior should converse with him with a show of regard for 
him and with his body bent_ forward (respectfully). 
He should not stand too 
near or sway his arms. 
He should never at any place put his arms round a boy's body and 
console him. 
He should recite [and learn the scriptures] without disturbing those in the 
· Hall of meditation . .. 
As it is stated 6 'when admitting [persons J into the priesthood, admit them 
after examination, ordain them after examination, give them (your) protection 
after examination. 
For, when even one son of a respectable family receives 
admission into the priesthood and (subsequently) the upasampadii ordination, 
he is instrumental in the establishment of even the whole Buddhist church'. 
Therefo,re, admission into the Buddhist Order should be made after examination. 
Likewise the upasampadii ordination as well as the nissaya protection <?ught 
to be conferred after examination. 
One should cultivate the Dhntanga 7 
ascetic practices as much as one can. 
No ill shall be spoken [ of any one J for unwillingly observing these aforesaid 
duties.

ROCK-INSCRIPTION 
OF PARAKKAMA-BAHU 
I 
Whosoever conducts himself in disobedience to and in violation of the 
disciplinary injunctions which have thus been enacted, shall receive the punish-
ment due to the offence committed and be warned. 
When this has been done three times successively and the bhikkhu still 
continues his misbehaviour in the selfsame manner, he shall not be given nissaya 
protection, but, after letting him .remain (in -the monastery) a month, if his 
demeanour be not in accordance with the Vinaya precepts, he should be expelled, 
and no one should hold communion with him. 
Likewise, if the Theras 
who are heads of chapters of monks should 
neglect their respective duties and [ as a result] fail to bring their community 
of bhikkhus under discipline, they should receive the punishments determined 
by the Senior Theras.

The language ~s in keeping with the style of Kitti Nissail.ka-Malla's 
other records ; the phraseology of the first line like that of the first three lines 
of his Dambulla inscription being copied from earlier epitaphs either of Vijaya-
Bahu I or of Parakkama-Bahu 
I 1. 
Tne contents are practically the same as those of many other gal-asana 
records of Nissailka-Malla, forming as they do, only the oft-repeated bombastic 
account of his military achievements and charitable acts by way of an introduc-
tion to the principal statement, indicating that the stone seat on which the 
present epitaph is engraved, ·was the one that His Majesty Kitti Nissanka-Malla, 
after his return from the Indian campaign, used to occupy whilst witnessing the 
various diversions such as alms-giving, dancing, singing, &c., in the Parvati-
satra erected at this king's request in Caturveda-Brahmapura, 'the city of 
the· F our-V edic Brahmans '. 
The inscription is not dated, but from the references to his tours of 
inspection and his alleged expedition to India, we may class it among those 
records indited at about the end of his short but eventful reign of nine years 
(1187-1196). 
In the articles on the Pritidanaka-maQ<;iapa and on Sahasamalla's 
slab, 
above Nos. 29 and 36, we put together all the information then available 
regarding Kitti Nissanka-Malla's lineage, his bz'ruda titles, and his career. 
The 
present record gives nothing fresh, save the reference to a Parvati-satra built in 
Caturveda-Brahmapura. 
The former was probably an alms-hall established in 
honour or memory either of his mother Parvati Mahadevi 2 or of Her Highness 
Parvati mentioned in the Hatadage wall-inscription 3• 
If Kantalai is the original site of the present gal-iisana, then this locality 
must have been once the town called Caturveda-Brahmapura, 
probably 
occupied mostly by Brahman families for whose benefit an almshouse ·called 
Brahma:Q.a-satra was also established by this King Nissanka-Malla 4.

TRANSLATION. 
[Lines 1-4] The illustrious monarch Kali:iigu Perakumba 1, abounding 
in a multitude of virtuous qualities which are pre-eminent in the boundless 
world; lord by (right of his) lineal descent from the lords 2 of the soil of the 
Island of Larika, who were descended from the race of King Vijaya, that threw 
into shade the other K~atriya races of Dambadiva 3, and that made Larika 
a habitation for man by extirpating the yak~as ; [His Majesty J who is gloriously 
endowed with qualities which are manifold, deep, majestic, unchangeable and 
gentle, [rich as] the Lord of wealth 4 (Kubera), of kingly mien, floodlike in gifts 5 
and sympathetic for the happiness of living beings,6 was pleased to make tours 7 
throughout prosperous Larika, inspect it thoroughly as if it were a ripe nelli fruit 
on the palm of his hand 8 and free it from the thorns of lawlessness. 
[His Majesty, moreover], gave security to animal life 9 in great tanks, 
remitted for all times the taxes pisatnburu-vata 
10 and kati-ada 11 and enacted that 
taxes should not be levied exceeding one amztJJa u and three pa{a 12 [in grain J
